## 9.2 On self-orthogonality and the closure relations

The spectrum of an $N \times N$ complex symmetric matrix $\mathbf{H}(\lambda)$ is complete when the closure relation is satisfied. $\lambda$ is a real or complex parameter and it is given that for $\lambda \neq \lambda_{bp}$ , N orthonormal eigenvectors are obtained,

$$
\mathbf {H} (\lambda) \mathbf {c} _ {j} (\lambda) = E _ {j} \mathbf {c} _ {j} (\lambda)\tag{9.36}
$$

such that

$$
[ \mathbf {C} (\lambda) \mathbf {C} ^ {\mathrm{T}} (\lambda) ] _ {N \times N} = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} | \mathbf {c} _ {j}) (\mathbf {c} _ {j} | = \mathbf {I} _ {N \times N},\tag{9.37}
$$

where $\mathbf{C}(\lambda)=(\mathbf{c}_{1}(\lambda),\mathbf{c}_{2}(\lambda),\ldots,\mathbf{c}_{j}(\lambda)\ldots,\mathbf{c}_{N}(\lambda))$ is the eigenvector matrix of $\mathbf{H}(\lambda)$ . At the critical value of $\lambda=\lambda_{bp}$ the spectrum is not complete since at least two linearly independent eigenvectors reduce to one. Let us assume that $N_{bp}$ eigenvectors of $\mathbf{H}(\lambda)$ coalesce at $\lambda=\lambda_{bp}$ . The number of linearly independent eigenvectors of the $N\times N$ matrix $\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})$ is

$$
M = N - N _ {\mathrm{bp}},\tag{9.38}
$$

such that for the $\{\mathbf{c}_{i = 1,2,\dots,M}\}$ eigenvectors that are associated with the eigenvalues $\{E_i(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})\}_{i = 1,\dots,M}$ ,

$$
(\mathbf {c} _ {i} | \mathbf {c} _ {i}) = \mathbf {c} _ {i} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {i} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = 1,\tag{9.39}
$$

while for the $[M = N - N_{\mathrm{bp}}]$ self-orthogonal eigenvector which is associated with the eigenvalue $E_{\mathrm{bp}}$ ,

$$
(\mathbf {c} _ {M + 1} | \mathbf {c} _ {M + 1}) = [ \mathbf {c} _ {M + 1} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) ] ^ {\mathrm{T}} [ \mathbf {c} _ {M + 1} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) ] = 0.\tag{9.40}
$$

In order to emphasize the fact that $\mathbf{c}_{M+1}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})$ is a self-orthogonal vector we may re-label it as

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) \equiv \mathbf {c} _ {M + 1} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}).\tag{9.41}
$$

It is clear that for $\lambda = \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}$ Eq. (9.37) is not satisfied and

$$
\mathbf {C} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) \mathbf {C} ^ {\mathrm{T}} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) \neq \mathbf {I} _ {N \times N}.\tag{9.42}
$$

As we will show below, it is possible to construct the closure relations by adding $N_{bp} - 1$ vectors $\{\mathbf{c}_{i}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})\}_{i=M+2,\ldots,N}$ to the $M + 1$ eigenvectors of $\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})$ . Let us first explain how these additional $N_{bp} - 1$ vectors can be computed and only afterwards we will explain why these vectors enable the calculations of the closure relations.

The desired N vectors construct an $N \times N$ matrix

$$
\mathbf {B} _ {N \times N} = (\mathbf {c} _ {1} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}), \dots , \mathbf {c} _ {M} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}), \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}), \mathbf {c} _ {M + 2} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}), \dots , \mathbf {c} _ {N} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}))\tag{9.43}
$$

which can be used to decompose $\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})$ into two blocks, $A_{M\times M}$ and $J_{N_{bp}\times N_{bp}}$ . The first matrix is a diagonal matrix whereas the second matrix is non-diagonalizable. That is,

$$
\mathbf {B H} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) \mathbf {B} ^ {- 1} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \mathbf {A} & \mathbf {0} \\ \mathbf {0} & \mathbf {J} \end{array} \right).\tag{9.44}
$$

The diagonal matrix A contains the eigenvalues of H while the non-diagonalizable matrix J has only two non-zero diagonals. The main diagonal $J_{i,i} = E_{bp}$ and the elements on the upper-diagonal are equal to 1, $J_{i,i+1} = 1$ . The closure relations for the whole N-dimensional space are given by

$$
\mathbf {I} _ {N \times N} = \mathbf {B} [ \mathbf {B} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {B} ] ^ {- 1} \mathbf {B} ^ {\mathrm{T}} = (\mathbf {c} _ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {c} _ {N}) \mathbf {U} (\mathbf {c} _ {1}, \dots , \mathbf {c} _ {N}) ^ {\mathrm{T}} = \sum_ {i, j = 1} ^ {N} U _ {i, j} | \mathbf {c} _ {i}) (\mathbf {c} _ {j} |.\tag{9.45}
$$

Note that for the Hermitian case $B^{T} = B^{-1}$ .

The question now is: how can we calculate the additional $N_{bp} - 1$ vectors $\{\mathbf{c}_{M+r}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})\}_{r=2,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ ? This can be done by solving the following linear set of equations:

$$
\begin{array}{l} {[ \mathbf {H} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \mathbf {I} ] \mathbf {c} _ {M + 2} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}),} \\ {[ \mathbf {H} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \mathbf {I} ] \mathbf {c} _ {M + 3} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = \mathbf {c} _ {M + 2} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}),} \end{array}
$$

$$
[ \mathbf {H} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \mathbf {I} ] \mathbf {c} _ {N - 1} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = \mathbf {c} _ {N} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}})\tag{9.46}
$$

such that all the $N_{bp}$ vectors $\{\mathbf{c}_{M+r}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})\}_{r=1,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ are degenerate eigenvectors of the same $N \times N$ matrix,

$$
[ \mathbf {H} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \mathbf {I} ] ^ {N _ {\mathrm{bp}}} \mathbf {c} _ {M + r} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = 0 \cdot \mathbf {c} _ {M + r} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}),\tag{9.47}
$$

where

$$
r = 1, 2, \dots , N _ {\mathrm{bp}}.\tag{9.48}
$$

Note that for the block associated with the almost self-orthogonal vectors $\lim_{\lambda\to\lambda_{bp}}[\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{bp})-E_{bp}\mathbf{I}]^{N_{bp}}=0$ and therefore we should multiply the $[\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{bp})-E_{bp}\mathbf{I}]$ matrices one by one by the vectors $\mathbf{c}_{M+r}(\lambda_{bp})$ .

The orthonormal eigenvectors of $\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})$ , denoted above as $\{c_{i=1,2,\ldots,M}\}$ , are also eigenvectors of the $N \times N$ matrix $[\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}) - E_{\mathrm{bp}}\mathbf{I}]^{N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ ,

$$
[ \mathbf {H} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \mathbf {I} ] ^ {N _ {\mathrm{bp}}} \mathbf {c} _ {i} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = [ E _ {i} - E _ {\mathrm{bp}} ] ^ {N _ {\mathrm{bp}}} \cdot \mathbf {c} _ {i} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}),\tag{9.49}
$$

where

$$
i = 1, 2, \ldots , N.\tag{9.50}
$$

We show here that $\mathbf{B} = (\mathbf{c}_{1}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}), \ldots, \mathbf{c}_{N}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}))$ is an $N \times N$ eigenvector matrix of the $N \times N$ matrix $[\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}) - E_{\mathrm{bp}}\mathbf{I}]^{N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ . Since the non-degenerate eigenvectors of the matrix are orthogonal it is clear that the additional vectors $\{\mathbf{c}_{M+r}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})\}_{r=2,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ are orthogonal to $\{\mathbf{c}_{i}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})\}_{i=1,\ldots,M}$ . Therefore, if we prove that $\{\mathbf{c}_{M+r}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})\}_{r=2,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ are linearly independent it implies that the spectrum of $[\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}) - E_{\mathrm{bp}}\mathbf{I}]^{N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ is complete while the spectrum of $\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})$ is not. The proof is simple. If $c_{M+2} = \alpha c_{bp}$ then from the first linear equation in Eq. (9.46) one gets the impossible result that $c_{bp} = 0$ . So, $c_{M+2}$ and $c_{bp}$ are two linearly independent vectors. Moreover, we can conclude also that $c_{M+2}$ is not an eigenvector of $[\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}) - E_{\mathrm{bp}}\mathbf{I}]$ . This conclusion together with the second linear equation in Eq. (9.46) leads us to another conclusion that $c_{M+3} \neq \alpha c_{M+2}$ . From similar arguments one can reach the conclusion that indeed $\{\mathbf{c}_{M+r}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})\}_{r=2,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ are linearly independent and therefore one can use the eigenvectors of $[\mathbf{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}) - E_{\mathrm{bp}}\mathbf{I}]^{N_{\mathrm{bp}}}$ to construct the closure relations (identity operator when the operator is represented by a finite matrix). On the basis of the derivation given above the closure relations in the $N_{bp}$ -dimensional subspace of the self-orthogonal vectors are given by

$$
\mathbf {I} _ {N _ {\mathrm{bp}} \times N _ {\mathrm{bp}}} = \sum_ {i = M + 1} ^ {N} \frac {| \mathbf {c} _ {i + 1} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}})) (\mathbf {c} _ {i} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) |}{(\mathbf {c} _ {i + 1} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) | \mathbf {c} _ {i} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}))}.\tag{9.51}
$$

For the case where two eigenstates coalesce as $\lambda \rightarrow \lambda_{bp}$ it is easy to see that for $N_{bp} = 2$ ,

$$
\mathbf {I} _ {N _ {\mathrm{bp}} \times N _ {\mathrm{bp}}} = \frac {| \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}}) (\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {*} | + | \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {*}) (\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} |}{(\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {*} | \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}})}\tag{9.52}
$$

since $c_{bp}$ is an eigenvector of a Hermitian matrix

$$
\mathcal {H} = (\mathbf {H} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \mathbf {I}) ^ {*} (\mathbf {H} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \mathbf {I})\tag{9.53}
$$

and therefore the scalar product should be used. Specifically,

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathcal {H} | \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}}) = 0 | \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}}),} \\ & {(\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {*} | \mathcal {H} = 0 (\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {*} |.} \end{array}\tag{9.54}
$$

## Exercise 9.6

(a) Show how the eigenvectors of the $2 \times 2$ matrix given in Eq. (9.10) which has an incomplete spectrum when $\lambda = i$ , can be used to construct the identity matrix $\mathbf{I}_{2 \times 2}$ .

(b) Similarly, show how the two linearly independent eigenvectors of the $3 \times 3$ matrix

$$
\mathbf {H} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 6 & \mathrm{i} & - 1 \\ \mathrm{i} & 5 & 2 \mathrm{i} \\ - 1 & 2 \mathrm{i} & 1 \end{array} \right)\tag{9.55}
$$

can be used to construct the identity matrix $\mathbf{I}_{3\times 3}$ .

It should be mentioned here that in numerical diagonalization calculations, due to round-off errors, the eigenvectors obtained are only nearly degenerate and can always be normalized to unity. Thus the spectrum of the matrix is always complete and there is no need to use the special closure relations given in Eq. (9.46) even when two or more eigenvectors coalesce. The same derivations and formulas which are given above for the closure relations hold for operators and are not limited to linear algebra where the operators are represented by finite matrices.

## 9.2.1 On self-orthogonality for complex potentials

Let us continue our discussion here by using a simple illustrative analytically soluble problem of a particle in a one-dimensional box with length L, where within the interval 0 < x < a, (a < L) a complex potential $V_{0}$ is introduced. That is,

$$
V (R) = \left\{ \begin{array}{c l} V _ {0} = v _ {0} - \mathrm{i} \Gamma  , & 0 <   R \leq a  , \\ 0  , & a <   R \leq L  , \\ \infty  , & o t h e r w i s e  . \end{array} \right.\tag{9.56}
$$

$v_{0}$ and $\Gamma$ are real parameters that model the electronic resonance's position and width. In this model the eigenvalues of the complex Hamiltonian are a function of three parameters, $E_{\nu}(a,v_{0},\Gamma)$ .

This simple 1D model potential shows how the original n-th particle-in-a-box wavefunction is deformed to be a self-orthogonal state when the complex $V_{0}$ potential parameter is varied. We will show here how the values of $V_{0} = v_{0} - i\Gamma$ for which a self-orthogonal state is obtained vary with the potential parameter a. It is a point of interest that this simple model problem can be associated with the propagation of light in a waveguide with a complex index of refraction. Last but not least, we will show here how the existence of a self-orthogonal state effects different measurable quantities.

In Chapter 3 we solved this problem for real $V_{0}$ . However, for the sake of coherence we remind the reader that due to the continuity condition at x = a,

$$
\sin (k a) = A \sin (q (a - L)),\tag{9.57}
$$

and the flux continuity condition at $x = a$ ,

$$
k \cos (k a) = A q \cos (q (a - L)),\tag{9.58}
$$

where

$$
\frac {(\hbar k) ^ {2}}{2 M} = E - v _ {0} + \mathrm{i} \Gamma\tag{9.59}
$$

and

$$
\frac {(\hbar q) ^ {2}}{2 M} = E.\tag{9.60}
$$

Let us prove that for given potential parameters a, L and $v_{0}$ , when we change $\Gamma$ from zero to $\infty$ then the spectrum of the one-dimensional particle in a box of length L transforms to a linear combination of two independent spectra associated with a particle in a box with length L - a and a particle in another box with length a. That is, as $\Gamma$ changes from 0 to $\infty$ then the energies

$$
E _ {n} = \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\frac {\hbar n \pi}{L}\right) ^ {2}; \quad n = 1, 2, \dots\tag{9.61}
$$

![](images/1bd78430ec0eb212d3167e26c8d026af7affa1b3bcea41563b9d6cbc7da06307.jpg)
Figure 9.1 The $\Gamma$ -trajectory of the first four eigenvalues of the model potential (solutions of Eq. (9.63)) with $L = \pi/\sqrt{2}$ and $a = L/\sqrt{3}$ . Atomic units are used throughout.

change to

$$
E _ {n ^ {\prime}, n ^ {\prime \prime}} = \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\frac {\hbar n ^ {\prime} \pi}{L - a}\right) ^ {2} + \frac {1}{2 M} \left(\frac {\hbar n ^ {\prime \prime} \pi}{a}\right) ^ {2} + v _ {0} - \mathrm{i} \Gamma ; \quad n ^ {\prime}, n ^ {\prime \prime} = 1, 2, \dots\tag{9.62}
$$

This can be easily shown by substituting Eqs. (9.59) and (9.60) into the following transcendental equation:

$$
\frac {q}{k} \tan (k a) = \tan (q (a - L))\tag{9.63}
$$

and taking the limit $\Gamma \to \infty$ , which yields the equality

$$
\mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \pi / 4} \sqrt {\frac {E}{\Gamma}} \tan (k a) = \tan (q (a - L)).\tag{9.64}
$$

As $\Gamma \to \infty$ the left-hand side of Eq. (9.64) vanishes (assuming that $ka \neq \pi(n + 1/2)$ , where $n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$ ) and therefore $\tan(q(a - L)) = 0$ . Consequently, $q(L - a) = n''\pi$ and $E_{n'} = (\hbar q)^2/(2M) = [(\hbar n')/(L - a)]^2/[2M]$ . By substituting this result into Eq. (9.57) one gets that $\sin(ka) = 0$ and therefore $ka = n''\pi$ . Consequently, $E_{n''} = (\hbar k)^2/(2M) = (\hbar n'')^2/(2Ma^2) + v_0 - i\Gamma$ and we have the two contributions in Eq. (9.64).

Let us visualize this result by solving Eq. (9.63) for the case where $a = L/\sqrt{3}$ and $v_{0} = 0$ . Figure 9.1 shows the changes in the complex eigenvalues with the variation in $\Gamma$ obtained for $L = \pi/\sqrt{2}$ . For $\Gamma = 0$ the eigenvalues of our model Hamiltonian are the energies of a particle in a box of size L. As $\Gamma$ is increased the eigenvalues depart from the real axis and penetrate into the complex energy plane. For sufficiently large values of $\Gamma$ some of the eigenvalues form a loop and return to the real axis, while others move almost tangentially to straight lines parallel to the imaginary axis. In complete agreement with the analysis given above, in the limit of $\Gamma \rightarrow \infty$ the spectrum of our model Hamiltonian is a superposition of two spectra where each of them is associated with a different problem. One spectra is that of a Hamiltonian of a particle in a box of size a, which is shifted into the complex energy plane by an imaginary constant $-i\Gamma$ . The corresponding eigenfunctions are given by

![](images/05876e1a3b5be9eb0d2f0af0d48bce7d927546f07ac903be50c3908321229d2a.jpg)
Figure 9.2 The $\Gamma$ -trajectory of the first four eigenvalues of the model potential (solutions of Eq. (9.63)) with $L = \pi/\sqrt{2}$ and a = L/2. Atomic units are used throughout. The inset shows the formation of branch points as $\Gamma$ is varied.

$$
\Psi_ {n} (x) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\Gamma t}{\hbar}} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i}}{\hbar} \left[ \frac {(\hbar n \pi) ^ {2}}{2 M a ^ {2}} - v _ {0} \right] t} \sqrt {\frac {2}{a}} \sin \left(\frac {n \pi x}{a}\right).\tag{9.65}
$$

The eigenfunctions have a nodal structure and their amplitudes decay to zero with the same rate as time passes. The other spectrum is that of a particle in a box of size L - a. Specifically, $E_{m} = (\hbar m\pi/(L - a))^{2}/(2M)$ and the corresponding eigenfunctions are stationary solutions given by

$$
\Psi_ {m} (x) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- \frac {\mathrm{i}}{\hbar} \left[ \frac {(\hbar m \pi) ^ {2}}{2 M (L - a) ^ {2}} \right] t} \sqrt {\frac {2}{L - a}} \sin \left(\frac {m \pi x}{L - a}\right).\tag{9.66}
$$

In Fig. 9.2 we present the result of $\Gamma$ -trajectory calculations for the case where $a = L / 2$ and $v_{0} = 0$ . In this special case each pair of initial eigenvalues (obtained for $\Gamma = 0$ ) associated with the quantum numbers $(n,n + 1)$ , where $n = 1,3,5,\ldots$ , coalesce in the complex energy plane as $\Gamma$ is increased. Each pair of eigenstates merges at a different critical value of $\Gamma_{(n,n + 1)}^{\mathrm{bp}}$ . Each time $\Gamma$ exceeds such a critical value a new pair of solutions is obtained. One of every pair of the new-born eigenvalues returns to the real energy axis as $\Gamma \rightarrow \infty$ whereas the other solution approaches a complex value with the same real part and an imaginary part which approaches $-i\Gamma$ . In the more general case where $a \neq L/2$ branch points are not obtained for $v_{0} = 0$ and only for very critical values of $v_{0}$ (and $\Gamma$ ) the spectrum become incomplete and two eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenfunctions coalesce. The values of $v_{0} = v_{0}^{bp}$ for which branch points are obtained due to the coalescence of two eigenfunctions were calculated by using the method of Byers Brown presented in the solution of Ex. 9.4 and in Section 9.1.1. Let us re-emphasize that, as $\Gamma \rightarrow \Gamma_{bp}$ ,

$$
\| E _ {1} - E _ {2} \| \to 0\tag{9.67}
$$

and also

$$
\| \Psi_ {1} (x) - \Psi_ {2} (x) \| \rightarrow 0,\tag{9.68}
$$

where $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ are the solutions of Eq. (9.63) obtained by using the definitions for $k$ and $q$ as given respectively in Eqs. (9.59) and (9.60). The wavefunctions $\Psi_{1}(x)$ and $\Psi_{2}(x)$ are obtained from Eq. (9.71).

In Fig. 9.3 we show how the two eigenfunctions change with the increase in $\Gamma$ . At the branch point the two orthogonal eigenfunctions become equal to one another and they reduced to a single self-orthogonal state. We can use this property, i.e.,

$$
(\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = \int_ {0} ^ {L} \mathrm{d} x \Psi^ {2} (x; E = E _ {\mathrm{bp}}) = 0,\tag{9.69}
$$

to derive a condition which must be satisfied at the branch points. By substituting the eigenfunctions of our model Hamiltonian which are given by (see Chapter 3)

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Psi (0 \leq x <   a) = \sin (\sqrt {2 M (E - v _ {0} + \mathrm{i} \Gamma)} x), \\ \Psi (a \leq x \leq L) = \left[ \frac {\sin (\sqrt {2 M (E - v _ {0} + \mathrm{i} \Gamma)} a)}{\sin (\sqrt {2 M E} (a - L))} \right] \sin (\sqrt {2 M E} (x - L)) \end{array}\tag{9.70}
$$

into Eq. (9.69) and using the value of $A^{2}$ given in Eq. (9.57), one gets that self-orthogonal states which are associated with a branch point in the complex energy plane are the solutions of the following equation:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left(\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} \mid \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}\right) \\ = \left[ \frac {L - a}{2} - \frac {\sin (2 q (L - a))}{4 q} \right] \left(\frac {k}{q}\right) ^ {2} \left(\frac {\cos^ {2} (k a)}{\cos^ {2} (q (L - a))}\right) + \frac {a}{2} - \frac {\sin (2 k a)}{4 k} = 0. \end{array}\tag{9.71}
$$

![](images/aae3bd50016618dbbf59833dd935bd38d661becd660490d74ed45ba54a16aa72.jpg)
Figure 9.3 The absolute value of the first two eigenfunctions of the model potential, $\Psi_{1}$ (full line) and $\Psi_{2}$ (dashed line) as a function of $\Gamma = 0, 1, 2, 3, 3.25, 3.5, 3.58, 3.6, 3.62$ and $3.627$ . $\Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}} = 3.627586692482452\ldots$ . Note how the functions start to resemble one another as $\Gamma$ approaches $\Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}}$ . Note that as $\Gamma \to \Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}}$ , $\Psi_{1} \to \Psi_{2}$ and a self-orthogonal state is obtained (see how the dashed and the full lines, which are very different when $\Gamma \ll \Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}}$ , become almost identical in the limit of $\Gamma \to \Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}}$ ).

This equation can be simplified by taking the value of $A^{2}$ from a combination of Eq. (9.57) and Eq. (9.58) and substituting into Eq. (9.72), yielding the following equation:

$$
(\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = q ^ {2} \left[ \frac {1 - \operatorname{sinc} (2 a k)}{\operatorname{sinc} (2 a k)} \right] - k ^ {2} \left[ \frac {1 - \operatorname{sinc} (2 (L - a) q)}{\operatorname{sinc} (2 (L - a) q)} \right] = 0,\tag{9.72}
$$

where $\operatorname{sinc}(\zeta) = \sin (\zeta) / \zeta$ .

What kind of information can be obtained from the calculations of the branch points in the complex energy plane? Below we list several consequences of the self-orthogonality phenomenon.

## 9.3 Calculations of the radius of convergence of perturbational expansion of the eigenvalues in $V_{0}$

Although we have already briefly mentioned in this chapter the relevance of self-orthogonality to the radius of convergence of the Taylor series expansion of a given function, for the sake of coherence and clarity let us extend our discussion on this subject. In the case that the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the full problem are calculated by the Rayleigh–Schrödinger perturbation theory where

$V_{0}$ is the perturbational expansion parameter, the radius of convergence, $R_{c}$ , is the smallest value of the absolute value of $V_{0}(bp)$ at which branch points in the complex energy plane are obtained. Note that this is also the radius of convergence of perturbational expansion of the eigenvalues within the framework of standard quantum mechanics when $V_{0}$ is real and the Hamiltonian is Hermitian. The Taylor expansions of the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions in $V_{0}$ are converged for the real and complex values of $V_{0}$ which are inside a circle of radius $R_{c}$ around $V_{0}=0$ .

## 9.4 The effect of self-orthogonality on c-expectation values

The potential parameters of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian are denoted by the vector $\lambda$ . The square integrable eigenfunctions are associated with complex non-degenerate eigenvalues. Without loss of generality we assume that the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian is a complex scaled Hamiltonian and that the square integrable non-degenerate eigenfunctions are the resonance wavefunctions,

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {H} _ {\theta} (\boldsymbol {\lambda}) | \Psi_ {j} (\boldsymbol {\lambda})) = E _ {j} (\boldsymbol {\lambda}) | \Psi_ {j} (\boldsymbol {\lambda}))  , \\ (\Psi_ {j ^ {\prime}} (\boldsymbol {\lambda}) | \Psi_ {j} (\boldsymbol {\lambda})) = \delta_ {j ^ {\prime}, j}  . \end{array}\tag{9.73}
$$

The vector of potential parameters can include, for example, the laser parameters (intensity and frequency) when the interaction with a laser field is taken into consideration. In such a case $\hat{H}_{\theta}(\lambda)$ stands for the complex scaled Floquet type operator (one should used the $(t, t')$ method when the laser field is not time-periodic).

For specific values of the real potential parameters, $\lambda = \lambda_{bp}$ , a branch point in the complex energy plane is obtained where the two corresponding eigenfunctions coalesce,

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {1} (\boldsymbol {\lambda} _ {\mathrm{bp}}) = E _ {2} (\boldsymbol {\lambda} _ {\mathrm{bp}}) \equiv E _ {\mathrm{bp}}, \\ | \Psi_ {1} (\boldsymbol {\lambda})) = | \Psi_ {2} (\boldsymbol {\lambda})) \equiv | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}). \end{array}\tag{9.74}
$$

The degeneracy of the two c-orthogonal functions implies that at the branch point a self-c-orthogonal (SO) state is obtained,

$$
(\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) = 0.\tag{9.75}
$$

We assume that the eigenfunctions of the Hermitian Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{\theta = 0}$ are real and therefore for $\theta \neq 0$ the c-product implies in this case that $(\Psi_{j'}(\pmb {\lambda})|\Psi_j(\pmb {\lambda})) = \langle [\Psi_{j'}(\pmb {\lambda})]^*\vert \Psi_j(\pmb {\lambda})\rangle$ and $(\Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}|\Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}) = \langle [\Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}]^*\vert \Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}\rangle$ .

By varying one of the potential parameters when all the others are held fixed at $\lambda = \lambda_{bp}$ , the degeneracy is removed from the spectrum and so is the SO phenomenon. Being sufficiently close to the SO conditions (i.e., $|(\lambda - \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})/\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}| \ll 1$ ),

$$
\begin{array}{l} {E _ {1} (\lambda) = E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}} + \beta (\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) + \dots} \\ {E _ {2} (\lambda) = E _ {\mathrm{bp}} - \alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}} + \beta (\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) + \dots ,} \end{array}\tag{9.76}
$$

where

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \Psi_ {1} (\lambda)) = \mathcal {N} _ {1} [ | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) + \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}}   | \chi) + (\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) | \xi) + \dots ] \\ | \Psi_ {2} (\lambda)) = \mathcal {N} _ {2} [ | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}}   | \chi) + (\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) | \xi) + \dots ]. \end{array}\tag{9.77}
$$

It is important to realize that in the above algebraic expansion the coefficient $\alpha$ and the function $|\chi\rangle$ are correspondingly a $\lambda$ -independent parameter and function. Let us give a graphic representation of the coalescence of the two almost degenerate eigenvalues $E_{1}(\lambda)$ and $E_{2}(\lambda)$ defined in Eq. (9.76), assuming that the coefficient $\alpha$ is complex. Sufficiently close to the branch point (the so-called exceptional point) the two complex almost-degenerate eigenvalues are

$$
\begin{array}{r} E _ {1} (\lambda) \simeq E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}}, \\ E _ {2} (\lambda) \simeq E _ {\mathrm{bp}} - \alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}}. \end{array}\tag{9.78}
$$

Assuming that the coefficient $\alpha$ is complex and both $\lambda$ and $\lambda_{bp}$ are real parameters, for a specific value of $\lambda = \lambda_{0}$ which satisfies $\lambda_{0} - \lambda_{bp} > 0$ we get that $E_{1}(\lambda_{0})$ and $E_{2}(\lambda_{0})$ are two points on a line in the complex energy plane where the branch point, $E_{bp}$ , lies on the mid-point (see Fig. 9.4). As $\lambda$ is increased the two eigenvalues move along the straight line towards the mid-point $E_{bp}$ and at the value of $\lambda = \lambda_{bp}$ the two coalesce. When $\lambda - \lambda_{bp} < 0$ the coefficient $\alpha$ is multiplied by $i = \exp(i\pi/2)$ and therefore as $\lambda$ is further reduced below $\lambda_{bp}$ the two almost-degenerate eigenvalues move along a line which is perpendicular to the previous line (see Fig. 9.4). We now move to examine the behavior of the corresponding eigenfunctions. Since the two almost-degenerate eigenfunctions are orthogonal,

$$
(\Psi_ {1} (\lambda)) | \Psi_ {2} (\lambda)) \cong \mathcal {N} _ {1} \mathcal {N} _ {2} [ \lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}} ] [ (\chi | \chi) + 2 (\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \xi) ] = 0,\tag{9.79}
$$

![](images/02dc8802ec8e3989c0a4d5a176ea93c1d64c161e909b4bd9ceeead4f6f01ad66.jpg)
Figure 9.4 A schematic representation of the coalescence of two almost-degenerate eigenvalues given in Eq. (9.78) as a real parameter in the Hamiltonian $\lambda$ is varied. The full circles stand for $E_{\pm}(\lambda_0) = \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}} + \delta$ , the open circles for $E_{\pm}(\lambda_0) = \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}} - \delta$ , where $\delta > 0$ , and the meeting-point of the arrows stands for $E_{\mathrm{bp}}$ . Note that for a real or imaginary value of the coefficient $\alpha$ the two almost-degenerate eigenvalues move along the two perpendicular lines such that for one of them $\operatorname{Re}(E_1(\lambda)) = \operatorname{Re}(E_2(\lambda))$ whereas for the second line $\operatorname{Im}(E_1(\lambda)) = \operatorname{Im}(E_2(\lambda))$ .

which implies that $(\chi |\chi)\cong -2(\Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}|\xi)$ . For sufficiently small values of $|\lambda -\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}|$ the complex normalization factors are chosen to be

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathcal {N} _ {1} ^ {2} \cong [ 2 (\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) ^ {1 / 2} (\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) ] ^ {- 1},} \\ & {\mathcal {N} _ {2} ^ {2} = - \mathcal {N} _ {1} ^ {2},} \end{array}\tag{9.80}
$$

such that

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\Psi_ {1} (\lambda) | \Psi_ {1} (\lambda)) = 1  , \\ (\Psi_ {1} (\lambda) | \Psi_ {1} (\lambda)) = 1  . \end{array}\tag{9.81}
$$

Therefore, as $(\lambda - \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}) \to 0$ , $N_{1} = iN_{2} \to \infty$ . As we will see later, this fact plays an important role in the large sensitivity of expectation values (using the c-product) to the potential parameters as the system approaches the SO conditions.

It is straightforward to see from Eq. (9.76)-(9.77) that the first derivatives of the resonance energy and the resonance widths which are associated with the almost-degenerate states $\Psi_{1}(\lambda)$ and $\Psi_{2}(\lambda)$ get infinitely large as $\lambda \rightarrow \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}$ . It is of particular interest to realize that sufficiently close to the SO conditions the decay rates of the resonance $\Gamma_{1} = -2\mathrm{Im}(E_{1})$ and $\Gamma_{2} = -2\mathrm{Im}(E_{2})$ associated with these states will show contrasting cusp-like behavior with respect to variation in $\lambda$ . $\Gamma_{1}$ will exhibit a sharp peak whereas $\Gamma_{2}$ will show a dip near the branch point.

It is also clear that the c-product expectation value of a complex scaled operator $\hat{O}_{\theta}$ which does not commute with the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in one of the almost SO states will be very large, such that

$$
\bar {O} _ {1} = \frac {(\Psi_ {1} (\lambda) | \hat {O} _ {\theta} | \Psi_ {1} (\lambda))}{(\Psi_ {1} (\lambda) | \Psi_ {1} (\lambda))} \to \infty ,
$$

$$
\bar {O} _ {2} = \frac {(\Psi_ {2} (\lambda) | \hat {O} _ {\theta} | \Psi_ {2} (\lambda))}{(\Psi_ {2} (\lambda) | \Psi_ {2} (\lambda))} \to \infty\tag{9.82}
$$

as $\lambda \rightarrow \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}$

The conclusion is that by adiabatically varying the potential parameters $\lambda$ , one can keep the system in one eigenstate and remain sufficiently close to the SO situation such that the expectation values of any operator that does not commute with the Hamiltonian will be very large. It implies, for example, that the standard deviation of any property which is represented by such an operator would be extremely large under these conditions. This means that one must vary the potential parameters sufficiently slowly to maintain the propagated wavepacket at a large overlap with one of the almost-SO states but almost orthogonal to the other SO state. Of course, at the branch point the adiabatic approach breaks down regardless of how slowly the potential parameters are varied.

Note, however, that although the resonance width has a finite value $\Gamma_{bp} = -2\text{Im}(E_{bp})$ , when $\lambda = \lambda_{bp}$ the first derivative of the resonance width, which is obtained by adiabatically varying the potential parameters, is increased as one gets closer to the SO conditions since from Eq. (9.76) one gets that

$$
\left| \frac {\partial \Gamma_ {1 , 2}}{\partial \lambda} \right| _ {\lambda = \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}} = \left| \frac {\partial (\Gamma_ {\mathrm{bp}} \mp 2 \mathrm{Im} [ \alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}} ])}{\partial \lambda} \right| _ {\lambda = \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}} = \infty .\tag{9.83}
$$

Here we vary only one real parameter $\lambda$ out of many potential parameters which are the components of $\lambda$ , where all other parameters are held fixed at the values at which the two eigenfunctions coalesce. This approach simplifies the representation and the analysis of the effects of being near the SO situation on measurable quantities.

Since near the branch point the two nearly degenerate states have similar wavefunctions, an important question is what the effect will be of the SO phenomenon on measurable quantities when the system is prepared in a wavepacket that populates both of them. That is, we what to see what happens if instead of populating one state we study a an initial complex scaled wavepacket, $|\Phi_{0}$ ), of the

form:

$$
\begin{array}{l} | \Phi_ {0}) = \sum_ {j = 1} a _ {j} | \Psi_ {j} (\lambda)), \\ a _ {j} = (\Psi_ {j} (\lambda) | \Phi_ {0}). \end{array}\tag{9.84}
$$

We use here the closure relation $\sum_{j=1}|\Psi_{j}(\lambda)(\Psi_{j}(\lambda)|$ which holds even when $\lambda$ is very close to $\lambda_{bp}$ where the spectrum is incomplete. When the complex scaled initial state is normalized to unity, $(\Phi_{0}|\Phi_{0})=1$ , then $\sum_{j=1}a_{j}^{2}=1$ although both $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ have very large complex values which increase as $|\lambda-\lambda_{bp}|$ decreases. Indeed, using Eqs. (9.76) and (9.80) one can see that

$$
a _ {1} ^ {2} + a _ {2} ^ {2} = 2 \frac {(\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Phi_ {0}) (\chi | \Phi_ {0})}{(\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}})}\tag{9.85}
$$

is a $\lambda$ -independent parameter. With the help of Eq. (9.89) we see that the leading term in the expansion of the expectation value of the mean energy of the wavepacket (WP) in $(\lambda - \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})$ is given by

$$
\begin{array}{l} \bar {E} _ {\mathrm{WP}} (\lambda) = (\Phi_ {0} | \hat {H} _ {\theta} | \Phi_ {0}) = \sum_ {j = 1} (\Psi_ {j} (\lambda) | \Phi_ {0}) ^ {2} E _ {j} (\lambda) \\ \simeq \frac {2 (\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Phi_ {0}) (\chi | \Phi_ {0})}{(\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}})} E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \frac {\alpha (\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Phi_ {0}) ^ {2}}{(\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}})} + \frac {\alpha (\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) (\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Phi_ {0}) ^ {2}}{(\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}})} \\ + \sum_ {j \neq 1, \neq 2} (\Psi_ {j} (\lambda) | \Phi_ {0}) ^ {2} E _ {j} (\lambda). \end{array}\tag{9.86}
$$

Here $\hat{H}_{\theta}$ stands for any non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and not necessarily for the complex scaled Hamiltonian. Note that, even when the last term in Eq. (9.86) can be neglected the third term in Eq. (9.86) is explicitly $\lambda$ -dependent for any case which is close to the SO situation, while the rest of the terms in the last expression can be $\lambda$ -independent. From Eq. (9.86) we conclude that the value of the complex mean energy is not very sensitive to the value of the potential parameters even when the system is very close to the SO situation. It is important to stress that here we assume that the initial state $\Phi_{0}$ is $\lambda$ -independent. The situation, of course, is very different when $\Phi_{0}$ changes adiabatically with $\lambda$ , as explained above.

The effect of the SO phenomenon on time-dependent measureable quantities. The discussion below is restricted to the cases where the time-dependent Schrödinger equation is solved for a complex potential (the situation where the physical potential is real and complex absorbing potentials are introduced to simplify the numerical calculations is excluded from this discussion).

The evolution in time of the complex scaled initial wavepacket, $\Phi_{0}$ , is given by

$$
| \Phi_ {0} (t)) = \sum_ {j = 1} a _ {j} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} E _ {j} (\lambda) t / \hbar} | \Psi_ {j} (\lambda)),\tag{9.87}
$$

where the coefficients $\{a_{j}\}_{j=1,2,\ldots}$ are given in Eq. (9.84). Using the F-product formalism presented in Chapter 6 we can calculate the probability of observing particles in the interaction region (in any finite volume in space) as a function of time,

$$
\rho (t) = \left| \sum_ {j = 1} a _ {j} ^ {2} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \Gamma_ {j} t / \hbar} \right|,\tag{9.88}
$$

where $\Gamma_{j} = -2\mathrm{Im}(E_{j})$ . When $|\lambda - \lambda_{bp}|$ is sufficiently large such that the system is far from the SO situation, then it is expected that the envelope of $\rho(t)$ will decay to zero, and when the initial WP mainly populates the longest living resonance state, $\Gamma_{1}$ , then $\mathrm{d}[\ln\rho(t)]/\mathrm{d}t \simeq \Gamma_{1}$ . As we will see below, the situation is very different when $|\lambda - \lambda_{bp}|$ is small so the system is very close to the SO situation. When $\lambda$ gets sufficiently close to $\lambda_{bp}$ then $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ are two almost-degenerate states (see Eq. (9.76)). Then $\Psi_{1}$ and $\Psi_{2}$ are orthonormal functions which have the form given in Eq. (9.77). Using Eqs. (9.76) and (9.80) one can see that

$$
\begin{array}{l} a _ {1} ^ {2} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \Gamma_ {1} t / \hbar} + a _ {2} ^ {2} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \Gamma_ {2} t / \hbar} \\ = F _ {-} (t) \left[ \frac {(\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Phi_ {0}) ^ {2}}{2 \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}} (\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}})} + \frac {(\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) (\chi | \Phi_ {0}) ^ {2}}{2 (\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}})} \right] + F _ {+} (t) \frac {(\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Phi_ {0}) (\chi | \Phi_ {0})}{(\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}})}, \end{array}\tag{9.89}
$$

where

$$
F _ {\pm} (t) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- \Gamma_ {\mathrm{bp}} t / \hbar} \left[ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{Im} (\alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}}) t / \hbar} \pm \mathrm{e} ^ {+ \mathrm{Im} (\alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}}) t / \hbar} \right].\tag{9.90}
$$

At t = 0 a $[\lambda - \lambda_{bp}]$ -independent result as given in Eq. (9.89) is obtained. As time passes more terms are involved in the dynamics and the dominant one is

$$
\frac {(\Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}} | \Phi_ {0}) ^ {2}}{2 (\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}}} \left[ \mathrm{e} ^ {- \Gamma_ {1} t / \hbar} - \mathrm{e} ^ {- \Gamma_ {2} t / \hbar} \right].\tag{9.91}
$$

It is quite clear that as the system is closer to the SO situation, although $\lim_{t\to\infty}\rho(t)=0$ there is a time interval $T_{1}<t<T_{2}$ for which

$$
\rho (t) \gg \rho (t = 0)\tag{9.92}
$$

and therefore as time passes presumably more particles have been created than initially introduced into the interaction region. How is it possible that when the system is close to the branch point the number of particles embedded inside the interaction region is increased? The answer to this question depends on the answer to another question. Are $\rho(t)$ and $|\Psi_{j}\rangle$ observable quantities? When the problem we solve is the scalar Maxwell equation within the paraxial approximation, where t in the time-dependent Schrödinger equation plays the role of the propagation axis Z of light in a waveguide and the potential energy term plays the role of the square of the spatial dependent index of refraction of the material, then $\rho(t = Z)$ is the power of the propagated light as function of Z. In such a case the $2 \times 2$ matrix

$$
\mathbf {H} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \epsilon - \mathrm{i} & 1 \\ 1 & + \mathrm{i} \end{array} \right)\tag{9.93}
$$

(which is equal to the matrix which has an incomplete spectrum and is given in Eq. (9.18) at time -i when $\epsilon = 0$ in Eq. (9.93)) is a model Hamiltonian of two coupled single-mode waveguides. One waveguide is constructed from a material which absorbs the propagated light and the rate of the loss of light power is $+2 = -2\mathrm{Im}(\epsilon - \mathrm{i})$ , whereas in the second waveguide there is a gain of power of the propagated light beam with a rate which is equal to $-2 = -2\mathrm{Im}(+\mathrm{i})$ . The off-diagonal Hamiltonian matrix elements stand for the couplings between the two optical modes. The calculations of $\rho(t)$ for an initial vector (1, 1) will show that for sufficiently small values of $\epsilon$ where two almost SO states are obtained one can find a time interval $T_{1} < t < T_{2}$ for which $\rho(t = Z) > \rho(0)$ .

However, when the time-dependent Schrödinger equation is solved both $\rho(t)$ and $|\Psi_{j}\rangle$ are not measurable quantities. Only expectation values stand for measurable quantities. Let us assume we wish to find the probability of detecting particles inside a box of volume $L^{3}$ as a function of time. When the initial (complex scaled) wavepacket is $\Phi_{0}$ , by using the F-product formalism this measurable quantity, which we denote by $P_{\mathrm{L}}(t)$ , is given by

$$
\begin{array}{c} P _ {\mathrm{L}} (t) = \left| \frac {\sum_ {j ^ {\prime} , j} a _ {j ^ {\prime}} a _ {j} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} (E _ {j} - [ E _ {j ^ {\prime}} ] ^ {*}) t / \hbar} \int_ {- L / 2} ^ {+ L / 2} \mathrm{d} \mathbf {r} \Psi_ {j ^ {\prime}} (\mathbf {r}) \Psi_ {j} (\mathbf {r})}{\sum_ {j ^ {\prime} , j} a _ {j ^ {\prime}} a _ {j} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} (E _ {j} - [ E _ {j ^ {\prime}} ] ^ {*}) t / \hbar} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {+ \infty} \mathrm{d} \mathbf {r} \Psi_ {j ^ {\prime}} (\mathbf {r}) \Psi_ {j} (\mathbf {r})} \right| \\ = \left| \frac {\sum_ {j ^ {\prime} , j} a _ {j ^ {\prime}} a _ {j} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} (E _ {j} - [ E _ {j ^ {\prime}} ] ^ {*}) t / \hbar} \int_ {- L / 2} ^ {+ L / 2} \mathrm{d} \mathbf {r} \Psi_ {{j ^ {\prime}}} (\mathbf {r}) \Psi_ {{j}} (\mathbf {r})}{\sum_ {j} a _ {j} ^ {2} \mathrm{e} ^ {- 2 \operatorname{Im} (E _ {j}) t / \hbar}} \right|, \end{array}\tag{9.94}
$$

where $\{a_j\}_{j = 1,2,\ldots}$ are defined in Eq. (9.84) and the non-measurable quantity $\rho (t)$ is given by

$$
\rho (t) = \left| \sum_ {j} a _ {j} ^ {2} \mathrm{e} ^ {- 2 \operatorname{Im} \left(E _ {j}\right) t / \hbar} \right|.\tag{9.95}
$$

Although $\rho(t)$ may grow in time, $P_{\mathrm{L}}(t=0) > P_{\mathrm{L}}(t>0)$ and the probability of finding the particles inside the box decays at all times, as it should.

## 9.5 Zero resonance contribution to the cross section

From the time-independent scattering theory presented in Chapter 8 we see that when a single resonance state controls the dynamics, the probability of a projectile with an energy E in an initial state denoted by $|i\rangle$ passing through a target to a specific final state denoted by $|f\rangle$ is approximately given by

$$
T _ {\mathrm{f,i}} (E) \simeq \left| \frac {\gamma_ {\mathrm{i}} ^ {\mathrm{res}} \gamma_ {\mathrm{f}} ^ {\mathrm{res}}}{E - E ^ {\mathrm{res}} + \mathrm{i} \Gamma / 2} \right| ^ {2},\tag{9.96}
$$

where up to phase factors, $e^{i\alpha_{i}}$ and $e^{i\alpha_{f}}$ , the coefficients $\gamma_{i}^{res}$ and $\gamma_{f}^{res}$ are the square roots of the partial widths. For the sake of simplicity let us discuss here the case where the system has two open channels for the decay and both of them have the same threshold energies. In such a case the two partial widths are identical,

$$
\gamma_ {\mathrm{i}} ^ {\mathrm{res}} = \gamma_ {\mathrm{f}} ^ {\mathrm{res}} = \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \varphi / 2} \sqrt {\Gamma / 2}.\tag{9.97}
$$

On the basis of the full transmission at resonance when $E = E^{res}$ , i.e., $T(E^{\mathrm{res}}) = 1$ , resonance tunneling diodes and transistors are produced. When the system is close to the condition for self-orthogonality, two resonances are nearly degenerate and thus, unlike the single resonance case, we get that

$$
\begin{array}{c} T (E) \simeq \left| \frac {\gamma_ {+} ^ {2}}{E - E _ {+} ^ {\mathrm{res}} + \mathrm{i} \Gamma_ {+} / 2} + \frac {\gamma_ {-} ^ {2}}{E - E _ {+} ^ {\mathrm{res}} + \mathrm{i} \Gamma_ {-} / 2} \right| ^ {2} \\ = \frac {1}{2} \left| \frac {\Gamma_ {+} / 2}{E - E _ {-} ^ {\mathrm{res}} + \mathrm{i} \Gamma_ {+} / 2} + \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} (\varphi_ {-} - \varphi_ {+})} \frac {\Gamma_ {-} / 2}{E - E _ {+} ^ {\mathrm{res}} + \mathrm{i} \Gamma_ {-} / 2} \right| ^ {2}. \end{array}\tag{9.98}
$$

The two resonance eigenvalues are given according to Eq. (9.76) by

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {\pm} ^ {\mathrm{res}} = \mathrm{Re} [ E _ {\mathrm{bp}} ] \pm \mathrm{Re} [ \alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}} ], \\ \Gamma_ {\pm} = - 2 \mathrm{Im} [ E _ {\mathrm{bp}} ] \mp 2 \mathrm{Im} [ \alpha \sqrt {\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}} ], \end{array}\tag{9.99}
$$

where $E_{bp}$ is the exceptional point in the spectrum which is associated with a branch point where two resonances coalesce with the change in the potential parameter $\lambda$ up to $\lambda_{bp}$ . A crucial point in our derivation is that the value of the relative phase factor $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}(\varphi_{-}-\varphi_{+})}$ is equal to -1. Another crucial point in our derivation is approaching the limit of $\lambda \rightarrow \lambda_{bp}$ when $\lambda \leq \lambda_{bp}$ , which is within the radius of convergence of the perturbational expansion in $\lambda$ . The reason for it is as follows. The partial width amplitudes, $\gamma_{\pm}^{2} = \exp(\mathrm{i}\varphi_{\pm})\Gamma_{\pm}/2$ , can be obtained by calculating the expectation values of the flux operator, $\gamma_{\pm}^{2} = (\Psi_{\pm}|\hat{\mathcal{F}}|\Psi_{\pm})$ , where the two nearly degenerate functions are given as in Eq. (9.77). That is, $\Psi_{+} \equiv \Psi_{1}(\lambda)$ and similarly $\Psi_{-} \equiv \Psi_{2}(\lambda)$ . From Eq. (9.77) one can see that as $\lambda \to \lambda_{bp}$ , $\Psi_{-} \to i\Psi_{+}$ and therefore $\gamma_{-}^{2} = -\gamma_{+}^{2}$ , which implies that indeed $e^{i(\varphi_{-}-\varphi_{+})} = -1$ . By substituting this result and Eqs. (9.99) into Eq. (9.98) one gets that

$$
\begin{array}{l} T (E, \epsilon) \\ \simeq \left| \frac {\operatorname{Im} \left(E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \epsilon\right)}{E - \operatorname{Re} \left(E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \epsilon\right) - \mathrm{i} \operatorname{Im} \left(E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \epsilon\right)} - \frac {\operatorname{Im} \left(E _ {\mathrm{bp}} - \epsilon\right)}{E - \operatorname{Re} \left(E _ {\mathrm{bp}} - \epsilon\right) - \mathrm{i} \operatorname{Im} \left(E _ {\mathrm{bp}} - \epsilon\right)} \right| ^ {2}, \end{array}\tag{9.100}
$$

where $\epsilon = \alpha\sqrt{\lambda - \lambda_{bp}}$ . From Eq. (9.100) one gets that the transition probability vanishes, $T(E, \epsilon) = 0$ , when $E = E_{0}(\epsilon)$ , which is given by

$$
\begin{array}{c} E _ {0} (\epsilon) = \frac {\operatorname{Im} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \epsilon) \operatorname{Re} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}} - \epsilon) - \operatorname{Im} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}} - \epsilon) \operatorname{Re} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \epsilon)}{\operatorname{Im} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}} + \epsilon) - \operatorname{Im} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}} - \epsilon)} \\ = \operatorname{Re} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}}) - \operatorname{Im} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}}) \frac {\operatorname{Re} (\epsilon)}{\operatorname{Im} (\epsilon)}. \end{array}\tag{9.101}
$$

Since the limit of $\epsilon\to0$ is obtained by taking the limit of $\lambda-\lambda_{bp}\leq0$ , $\lim_{\epsilon\to0}E_{0}(\epsilon)=\mathrm{Re}(E_{\mathrm{bp}})-\mathrm{Im}(E_{\mathrm{bp}})\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)/\mathrm{Re}(\alpha)$ and consequently, for the cases where $\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)$ (without loss of generality we assume here that $\lambda$ and $\lambda_{bp}$ get real values only) or $\mathrm{Im}(E_{\mathrm{bp}})$ gets sufficiently small,

$$
T (E = \mathrm{Re} (E _ {\mathrm{bp}}), \lambda \simeq \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}}) \simeq 0.\tag{9.102}
$$

For the special cases where $\alpha$ is real, $\mathrm{Re}(\epsilon)=\mathrm{Im}(\alpha)=0$ and the transition probability vanishes at the branch point.

## 9.6 Geometric phases (Berry phases)

The fact that for a certain set of potential parameters two (in principle it can be more than two) eigenfunctions coalesce is associated with a branch point in the complex energy plane (which is also known as an exceptional point). As discussed above, by holding fixed all the potential parameters except one (denoted by $\lambda$ ) the branch point is obtained at $\lambda = \lambda_{bp}$ , such that $E_{\pm} = E_{bp} \pm \alpha \sqrt{\lambda - \lambda_{bp}}$ for a real value of $\lambda_{bp}$ or $E_{\pm} = E_{bp} \pm \alpha \sqrt{(\lambda - \lambda_{bp})(\lambda - \lambda_{bp}^{*})}$ when $\lambda_{bp}$ is complex. Note that we can always extend the $\lambda$ -space to include the real and imaginary parts of the potential parameters separately (i.e., rather than N complex parameters in the vector $\lambda$ there can be 2N real parameters) so that without lost of generality we can study here the case where $\lambda_{bp}$ is a set of real parameters. We vary one parameter in the complex parameter space in a circle with radius R which is centered around $\lambda = \lambda_{bp}$ . That is, we change $\lambda$ such that

$$
\lambda - \lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}} = R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \phi}.\tag{9.103}
$$

We now wish to study how the energy and the corresponding eigenfunction change when $\phi$ is adiabatically varied from $\phi = 0$ to $\phi = 2n\pi$ , where $n = 1, 2, \ldots$ . If the circle is centered such that there are no branch points inside the circle then $E_{\pm}(\phi = 0) = E_{\pm}(\phi = 2n\pi)$ and $\Psi_{\pm}(\phi = 0) = \Psi_{\pm}(\phi = 2n\pi)$ . As we will see, the situation is very different when the path we choose encircles a branch point. By substituting Eq. (9.103) into Eqs. (9.76), (9.77) and (9.80) one gets that the energies are given by

$$
E _ {\pm} (\phi) \equiv E _ {\pm} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}} + R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \phi}) = E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \pm \alpha R ^ {1 / 2} \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \phi / 2}\tag{9.104}
$$

and the wavefunctions (assuming that the matrix is symmetric and therefore $(\Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}|\Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}) = \langle \Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}^{*}|\Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}\rangle = 0)$ are

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {| \Psi_ {+} (\phi)) \equiv | \Psi_ {+} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}} + R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \phi}))} \\ & {\qquad = R ^ {- 1 / 4} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \phi / 4} [ 2 (\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} [ | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) + R ^ {1 / 2} \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \phi / 2} | \chi) ],} \\ & {| \Psi_ {-} (\phi)) \equiv | \Psi_ {-} (\lambda_ {\mathrm{bp}} + R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \phi}))} \\ & {\qquad = \mathrm{i} R ^ {- 1 / 4} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \phi / 4} [ 2 (\chi | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} [ | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) - R ^ {1 / 2} \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \phi / 2} | \chi) ].} \end{array}\tag{9.105}
$$

From Eqs. (9.104) and (9.105) one can see that after one loop of $2\pi$ there is an exchange between the two almost-SO states,

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {\pm} (2 \pi) = E _ {\mp} (0), \\ | \Psi_ {\pm} (2 \pi)) = \mp | \Psi_ {\mp} (0)), \end{array}\tag{9.106}
$$

while after two loops the energy returns to its original value while the corresponding almost-degenerate eigenfunction accumulates a phase of $\pi$ ,

$$
\begin{array}{l} {E _ {\pm} (4 \pi) = E _ {\pm} (0),} \\ {| \Psi_ {\pm} (4 \pi)) = - | \Psi_ {\pm} (= 0)).} \end{array}\tag{9.107}
$$

Only after four loops do both the energy and the corresponding almost-SO eigenfunctions return to the initial energy and eigenfunction,

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {\pm} (8 \pi) = E _ {\pm} (0), \\ | \Psi_ {\pm} (8 \pi)) = | \Psi_ {\pm} (= 0)). \end{array}\tag{9.108}
$$

![](images/42a99e21ddccc791702a612134c7c5786ac48545c658600cb8fe28da5d49cfb8.jpg)
Figure 9.5 Adiabatic $\phi$ -trajectory in the parameter space $(\Gamma, a)$ for the complex eigenvalue of our model problem which is defined in Eq. (9.56) ( $v_0 = 0$ ). The trajectory starts at $\phi = 0$ and ends at $\phi = 2\pi$ . The loop $(\Gamma, a)$ is parameterized by the angle $\phi$ , where $\Gamma = \Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}} + R_{\Gamma} \cos \phi$ and $a = a_{\mathrm{bp}} + R_a \sin \phi$ . $R_{\Gamma} = 1.5$ , the branch point is at $\Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}} = 3.62758669 \ldots$ and $a_{\mathrm{bp}} = L/2$ ; $R_a = L/4$ . As one can see, the loop around the branch point shows a transition from one state to another. This happens when we are quite far from the branch point (the so-called exceptional point, EP).

The geometrical phases (known also as Berry phases) are the signs in Eqs. (9.107) and (9.108). Note that the situation is the same in the non-symmetric case since the transition from the symmetric to the non-symmetric is possible by carrying out the proper transformation (see, for example, the use of the Lanczos recursion method as described in Ex. 9.2). Note also that we discuss here the non-Hermitian degeneracy (i.e., self-orthogonality) which occurs when exploring one complex parameter, while in many cases (i.e., optics and laser physics) the non-Hermitian degeneracy typically occur when exploring two real parameters.

This important result can be verified for the illustrative model potential given in Eq. (9.56) without the need for R to be small.

In Fig. 9.5 we show the adiabatic $\phi$ -trajectory for the complex eigenvalue of our model problem.

Figure 9.6 shows the projection of $\Psi_{+}(x;R,\phi)$ for $0\leq \phi \leq 4\pi$ on the initial state $\Psi_{+}(x;R,0)$ (one of the almost self-orthogonal eigenfunctions). The projection has been carried out by the c-product where $(\Psi_{+}(x;R,0)|\Psi_{+}(x;R,\phi) = \langle \Psi_{+}^{*}(x;R,0)|\Psi_{+}(x;R,\phi)\rangle$ . As one can see, after one-loop the projection is equal to zero. It implies that after one-loop $\Psi_{+}\rightarrow \Psi_{-}$ . After two loops $\Psi_{+}\rightarrow -\Psi_{+}$ as we obtained from our analytical analysis. Only after four loops does $\Psi_{+}\rightarrow \Psi_{+}$ .

Let us consider a closed loop in the space of complex $V_{0}$ . This is to be distinguished from the previous calculations presented above for a loop in the parameter space $(\Gamma, a)$ .

(9.56). The trajectory starts at $\phi = 0$ and ends at $\phi = 8\pi$ . As one can see, after one-loop the projection is equal to zero. It implies that after one-loop $\Psi_{+} \to \Psi_{-}$ . After two loops $\Psi_{+} \to -\Psi_{+}$ as we obtained from our analytical analysis. Only after four loops does $\Psi_{+} \to \Psi_{+}$ .

As one can see, the loop around the branch point shows a transition from one state to another. This happens when we are quite far from the branch point.

In Fig. 9.7 we portray the variation of the eigenvalues in a loop $V_{0}(\phi) = V_{\mathrm{bp}} + R \exp(\mathrm{i}\phi)$ , where a is constant. The transition from a solid to a dashed line reflects the adiabatic transition from one eigenvalue to another as we complete the loop around the branch point at $V_{0} = V_{bp}$ .

Similarly, we show in Fig. 9.8 the variation of the eigenfunction, which corresponds to the eigenvalue in Fig. 9.7, as the phase $\phi$ is varied such that $V_{0}(\phi)$ forms a loop around the branch point $\Gamma_{bp}$ . The purpose of Fig. 9.7 and Fig. 9.8 is to show that the transition from one eigenstate to another takes place whenever an adiabatic variation in parameter space occurs in a closed loop around a branch point. This is regardless of the parameter space where the adiabatic variation calculations were performed.

![](images/f32f73d6d44b76fd257c399362207220fd54204997beab410303c33dd618d236.jpg)
Figure 9.8 The projection of the eigenfunction on the initial eigenfunction of our model potential which is defined in Eq. (9.56), obtained for $\phi = 0$ where $\phi$ is varied adiabatically (in $V_{0}$ complex parameter space). The trajectory starts at $\phi = 0$ and ends at $\phi = 8\pi$ .

Can we get an estimate for the SO state from the two states we obtain near the branch point? From Eqs. (9.80) and (9.77) we get that when $|\lambda - \lambda_{bp}|$ is sufficiently small

$$
| \Psi_ {1}) - \mathrm{i} | \Psi_ {2}) = 2 \mathcal {N} _ {1} | \Psi_ {\mathrm{bp}}) \equiv | \tilde {\Psi} _ {\mathrm{bp}}).\tag{9.109}
$$

Since $\Psi_{bp}$ is a self-orthogonal state of the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}(\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}})$ then so is $|\tilde{\Psi}_{bp})$ and $(\tilde{\Psi}_{\mathrm{bp}}|\tilde{\Psi}_{\mathrm{bp}})=0$ . Note that one can use different normalization conditions for the almost-SO states. For example, when the calculations are carried out by using a finite number of basis functions (based on the c-linear variational principle in Chapter 7) then $|\Psi_{1})$ and $|\Psi_{2})$ are normalized such that the largest dominant component in the basis set expansion is equal to unity. In such a case,

$$
| \Psi_ {1}) - | \Psi_ {2}) = | \tilde {\Psi} _ {\mathrm{bp}})\tag{9.110}
$$

such that

$$
(\tilde {\Psi} _ {\mathrm{bp}} | \tilde {\Psi} _ {\mathrm{bp}}) = 0.\tag{9.111}
$$

The conclusion is that a linear superposition of the two c-normalizable almost-SO eigenstates that are obtained for $\lambda \neq \lambda_{bp}$ converges to the SO state as $\lambda \rightarrow \lambda_{bp}$ faster than each of these states. Consider the situation when two parameters, $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ , should be varied in order to obtain an SO situation. For example, when an atom, a molecule or a nanostructure system interacts with a laser field the two parameters can be the laser field intensity and frequency. There are many ways to find the branch point (if it exists). Here we describe one method which is simple to implement and requires the calculations of the eigenvalues of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian only. First carry out adiabatic calculations when the two parameters are varied along a circle with radius R centered at $\lambda_{1}^{c}$ and $\lambda_{2}^{c}$ . That is,

$$
\begin{array}{l} \lambda_ {1} = \lambda_ {1} ^ {\mathrm{c}} + R \sin \varphi  , \\ \lambda_ {2} = \lambda_ {2} ^ {\mathrm{c}} + R \cos \varphi  , \end{array}\tag{9.112}
$$

where $0 \leq \varphi \leq 2\pi$ . Let us assume that for a sufficiently large value of R only a single branch point is embedded somewhere inside this circle. In such a case, when the adiabatic variation of $\varphi$ starts with the almost-degenerate eigenvalue $E_{1}(\varphi_{0})$ then by the end of the loop the second almost-degenerate eigenvalue will be obtained,

$$
E _ {1} (\varphi_ {0}) = E _ {2} (\varphi_ {0} + 2 \pi),\tag{9.113}
$$

and similarly,

$$
E _ {2} (\varphi_ {0}) = E _ {1} (\varphi_ {0} + 2 \pi).\tag{9.114}
$$

The next step in the calculations of $\lambda_{1}^{bp}$ and $\lambda_{2}^{bp}$ is to gradually reduce the radius such that for $R > R_{c}$ Eqs. (9.113) and (9.114) are satisfied but not for $R \leq R_{c}$ . It implies that the branch point is located somewhere on a circle that is centered around $(\lambda_{1}^{c}, \lambda_{2}^{c})$ in the 2D parameter plane with radius is $R = R_{c}$ . One should repeat these steps of the calculation where now the contour of the $\varphi$ -adiabatic calculations is a circle centered at $(\lambda_{1}^{c2}, \lambda_{2}^{c2}) = (\lambda_{1}^{c} + R_{c} \sin \varphi_{0}, \lambda_{2}^{c} + R_{c} \cos \varphi_{0})$ (the value of $\varphi_{0}$ can be taken arbitrarily between 0 and $2\pi$ ) and its radius $R \leq 2R_{c}$ is gradually reduced to a value $R_{c2}$ such that for $R > R_{c2}$ Eqs. (9.113) and (9.114) are satisfied but not for $R \leq R_{c2}$ . One of the two intersection points of the two circles is the desired branch point $(\lambda_{1}^{bp}, \lambda_{2}^{bp})$ . Namely, $\lambda_{1}^{bp}$ and $\lambda_{2}^{bp}$ are one pair out of the two pairs of solutions of the two coupled equations,

$$
\begin{array}{l} (\lambda_ {1} ^ {\mathrm{bp}} - \lambda_ {1} ^ {\mathrm{c}}) ^ {2} + (\lambda_ {2} ^ {\mathrm{bp}} - \lambda_ {2} ^ {\mathrm{c}}) ^ {2} = R _ {\mathrm{c}} ^ {2}, \\ (\lambda_ {1} ^ {\mathrm{bp}} - \lambda_ {1} ^ {\mathrm{c2}}) ^ {2} + (\lambda_ {2} ^ {\mathrm{bp}} - \lambda_ {2} ^ {\mathrm{c2}}) ^ {2} = R _ {\mathrm{c2}} ^ {2}. \end{array}\tag{9.115}
$$
