## Exercise 9.7

For the model Hamiltonian given in Eq. (9.10) show that a superposition of the two non-normalized almost-SO eigenvectors given in Eq. (9.12)

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{LC}} (\lambda) \equiv \frac {\mathbf {c} _ {+} (\lambda) + \mathbf {c} _ {-} (\lambda)}{\sqrt {2}} \rightarrow \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}}\tag{9.116}
$$

as $\lambda \rightarrow i$ , where $c_{bp}$ is a self-orthogonal vector which is associated with a branch point where the two eigenvectors merge. Moreover, prove that

$$
\left\{\frac {\partial}{\partial \lambda} \left| \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{LC}} (\lambda) \right| ^ {2} \right\} _ {\lambda = \mathrm{i}} = 0,\tag{9.117}
$$

while

$$
\left\{\frac {\partial}{\partial \lambda} \left| \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {\pm} (\lambda) \right| ^ {2} \right\} _ {\lambda = \mathrm{i}} = 2.\tag{9.118}
$$

For the simple analytical solvable problem with the complex 1D potential which is given in Eq. (9.56) we calculated the almost-SO states as functions of the potential parameter $\Gamma = \Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}} + R$ . $\Gamma$ is the potential parameter $\lambda$ that appears above in our discussion for the most general case and $\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}} = \Gamma_{\mathrm{bp}}$ , and therefore $\lambda - \lambda_{\mathrm{bp}} = R$ is the small parameter in our problem which determines how far the two almost SO states are from the branch point where they coalesce.

The results presented in Fig. 9.9 show clearly that for a broad range of values of R a linear combination of two eigenstates provides the self-orthogonal eigenfunctions (in a very good approximation). Moreover, the first derivative $\mathrm{d}[(\Psi_{\mathrm{bp}}|\Psi_{\mathrm{LC}}(R\equiv\lambda-\lambda_{\mathrm{bp}}))]/\mathrm{d}R=0$ at R=0. Note that here we omit the label “res” from the two almost-SO states and from the SO solution since the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in this case results from the use of a complex potential and because of the use of one of the complex scaling transformations that are applied for the calculation of the square integrable resonance states.

## Exercise 9.8

Consider a system interacting with a laser field with frequency $\omega_{L}$ and a maximum field amplitude of $\epsilon_{0}$ . Assume that for specific values of the field parameters $\epsilon_{0}^{bp}$ and $\omega_{L}^{bp}$ two resonance eigenvalues, $E_{\pm}$ , and their corresponding eigenvectors coalesce.

(1) Prove that the functional dependence close to the branch point of the two nearly degenerate resonance eigenvalues is given by

$$
E _ {\pm} = E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \pm \sqrt {a (\omega_ {\mathrm{L}} - \omega_ {\mathrm{L}} ^ {\mathrm{bp}}) + b (\epsilon_ {0} - \epsilon_ {0} ^ {\mathrm{bp}})}.\tag{9.119}
$$

(2) Now consider a straight line $\epsilon_0(\omega_{\mathrm{L}}) = \epsilon_0^{\mathrm{bp}} + \alpha (\omega_{\mathrm{L}} - \omega_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{bp}})$ , where $\alpha = -\frac{\operatorname{Im}(a)}{\operatorname{Im}(b)}$ , which passes through the branch point $(\omega_L^{\mathrm{bp}},\epsilon_0^{\mathrm{bp}})$ in the laser parameters' space. Show that close to the branch point along this line either the widths of the two resonance states $E_{\pm}$ are equal, i.e. $\operatorname{Im}(E_+) = \operatorname{Im}(E_-)$ , or their energy positions are equal, i.e. $\operatorname{Re}(E_+) = \operatorname{Re}(E_-)$ . At the branch point both of these conditions are satisfied and the two resonances are degenerate.

(3) Show that along the above-mentioned line in the $(\omega_{\mathrm{L}},\epsilon_0)$ parameter space, when $\omega_{\mathrm{L}}\geq \omega_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{bp}}$ , the resonance widths of $E_{\pm}$ are identical, i.e., $\operatorname {Im}(E_{+} - E_{-}) = 0$ , while when $\omega_{\mathrm{L}}\leq \omega_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{bp}}$ , $\operatorname {Re}(E_{+} - E_{-}) = 0$ .

(4) Show that the condition that $[\mathrm{Re}(E_{+}-E_{-})]^{2}=[\mathrm{Im}(E_{+}-E_{-})]^{2}$ is satisfied on the straight line $\epsilon_{0}(\omega_{\mathrm{L}})=\epsilon_{0}^{\mathrm{bp}}+\tilde{\alpha}(\omega_{\mathrm{L}}-\omega_{L}^{\mathrm{bp}})$ , where $\tilde{\alpha}=-\frac{\mathrm{Re}(a)}{\mathrm{Re}(b)}$ .

## 9.7 Concluding remarks

(1) The self-orthogonality (SO) condition implies that for specific and unique parameters two or more orthogonal eigenfunctions of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian coalesce and $(\Psi_{\mathrm{SO}}|\Psi_{\mathrm{SO}}) = 0$ , where the c-product is used. The coalescence happens at a branch point in the complex energy plane where the spectrum of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian becomes incomplete. This branch point is considered as an exceptional point in the energy spectrum.

(2) When the Hamiltonian is represented by a non-Hermitian finite $N \times N$ matrix, upon coalescence the number of linearly independent eigenvectors is smaller than N.

(3) The closure relations can be reconstructed from the SO state and the other eigenfunctions (eigenvectors) of the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian which has an incomplete spectrum by adding additional $N_{bp} - 1$ functions (vectors). $N_{bp}$ stands for the number of eigenfunctions (eigenvectors) which coalesce.

(4) The fingerprints of the SO phenomenon appear when the Hamiltonian has a complete spectrum but is sufficiently close to the SO situation that several (usually two) eigenfunctions (eigenvectors) are almost-SO states. Being almost-SO states implies that they are very much alike although they are orthogonal. By normalizing these states to unity their amplitudes (components of eigenvectors) become extremely large as one nears the SO situation.

(5) The self-orthogonal state can be recovered even when the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian has a complete spectrum and all eigenfunctions (eigenvectors) are normalizable.

(6) The effects of the SO phenomenon on observable quantities is measurable even when the spectrum of the non-Hermitian is complete and there is no SO eigenstate. These effects are hard or even impossible to predict by carrying out calculations within the framework of the Hermitian formalism of quantum mechanics.

## 9.8 Solutions to the exercises

## Answer to Exercise 9.1

This problem has been taken from a paper published by Moiseyev, Kventsel and Katriel. $^{12}$

The eigenvalues of the given matrix are obtained by taking $\det(\mathbf{H}-EI)=0$ , which leads to the following cubic equation for the characteristic polynomial:

$$
E ^ {3} - x E ^ {2} - \left(\frac {3 a ^ {2}}{2} + \frac {9}{1 6}\right) E + \left(x + \frac {7}{8}\right) a ^ {2} + \frac {x + 2}{1 6} = 0.\tag{9.120}
$$

The solutions of the cubic equation

$$
E ^ {3} + a _ {1} E ^ {2} + a _ {2} E + a _ {3} = 0\tag{9.121}
$$

depend on the discriminant, $D = Q^{3} + R^{2}$ , where Q and R are given by

$$
Q = \frac {3 a _ {2} - a _ {1} ^ {2}}{9}; \quad R = \frac {9 a _ {1} a _ {2} - 2 7 a _ {3} - 2 a _ {1} ^ {3}}{5 4}.\tag{9.122}
$$

For $a = 1 / \sqrt{2}$ we find that the coefficients of the cubic equation are $a_1 = -x$ , $a_2 = -21 / 16$ and $a_3 = 9(x + 1) / 16$ .

(1) A crossing of two eigenvalues is obtained when the discriminant is equal to zero. Substituting in the discriminant leads to a polynomial for $x$ with a root at $x = 1/4$ . Substituting $x = 1/4$ in the characteristic polynomial in Eq. (9.120) gives $a1 = -1/4$ , a2 = -21/16 and a3 = 45/64. The solutions to the cubic equation are given by

$$
E _ {1} = S + T - a _ {1} / 3,\tag{9.123}
$$

$$
E _ {2, 3} = (S + T) / 2 - a _ {1} / 3 \pm \mathrm{i} \sqrt {3} (S - T) / 2,\tag{9.124}
$$

where

$$
S = \sqrt [ 3 ]{R + D ^ {1 / 2}}; \qquad T = \sqrt [ 3 ]{R - D ^ {1 / 2}}.\tag{9.125}
$$

Since D = 0, in this case we get that S = T = -2/3. Accordingly, the eigenvalues at the crossing point are $E_{1} = -5/4$ , $E_{2} = 3/4$ and $E_{3} = 3/4$ .

(2) The plot of $|E_3(x) - E_2(x)|$ as function of $x$ exhibits a cusp at the point of crossing since the two eigenvalues at this point are equal.

(3) Any infinitesimally small change in the values of the matrix elements (as for example by changing $a$ to $a = 1 / \sqrt{2.001}$ ) will change the cusp behavior of $|E_3(x) - E_2(x)|$ to an analytical function with a minimum.

(4) By adding $1/4$ to the diagonal of $\mathbf{H}$ we get the same eigenvalues as for the matrix $\mathbf{M}$ . Therefore,

$$
\mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {M} \mathbf {U} = \mathbf {H} (x = 0. 2 5) + 0. 2 5 \mathbf {I}\tag{9.126}
$$

and the unitary matrix U is given by

$$
\mathbf {U} = \mathbf {C D} ^ {\mathrm{T}},\tag{9.127}
$$

where $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{D}$ are correspondingly the eigenvector matrices of $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{H}(x = 0.25) + 0.25\mathbf{I}$ which have the same eigenvalue spectra. That is, $\mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{M}\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{D}^{\mathrm{T}}[\mathbf{H}(x = 0.25) + 0.25\mathbf{I}]\mathbf{D}$ . The matrix $\mathbf{U}$ is obtained from Eq. (9.127),

$$
\mathbf {U} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 1 / 2 & a & 1 / 2 \\ a & 0 & - a \\ 1 / 2 & - a & 1 / 2 \end{array} \right)  ,\tag{9.128}
$$

where $a = 1/\sqrt{2}$ .

## Answer to Exercise 9.2

The $N \times N$ non-symmetric matrix is denoted by $\mathbf{H}$ and the transformed tri-diagonal symmetric matrix by $\mathbf{T}$ . The right and left Lanczos recursion vectors are defined as $\mathbf{U}^{\mathrm{L,R}} = \left(\mathbf{U}_1^{\mathrm{L,R}}, \mathbf{U}_2^{\mathrm{L,R}}, \dots, \mathbf{U}_N^{\mathrm{L,R}}\right)$ such that

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left[ \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{L}} \right] ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{R}} = \mathbf {I}, \\ \left[ \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{L}} \right] ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {H} \mathbf {U} ^ {\mathrm{R}} = \mathbf {T}, \\ \mathbf {H} \left[ \mathbf {U} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{L}}, \mathbf {U} _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{L}}, \dots , \mathbf {U} _ {N} ^ {\mathrm{L}} \right] = \left[ \mathbf {U} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{R}}, \mathbf {U} _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{R}} \dots , \mathbf {U} _ {N} ^ {\mathrm{R}} \right] \mathbf {T}, \end{array}\tag{9.129}
$$

where I is an $n \times N$ unit matrix and

$$
\begin{array}{l} T _ {n, n} \equiv \alpha_ {n}, \\ T _ {n, n + 1} \equiv T _ {n + 1, n} = \beta_ {n}. \end{array}\tag{9.130}
$$

By considering the sequence of vector multiplications $U_{1}^{L,R}$ , $U_{2}^{L,R}$ , $\ldots$ , $U_{N}^{L,R}$ onto H and T in Eq. (9.129) it is easy to see that

$$
\begin{array}{r} \mathbf {H} \mathbf {U} _ {n} ^ {\mathrm{R}} = \beta_ {n - 1} ^ {\mathrm{R}} \mathbf {U} _ {n - 1} ^ {\mathrm{R}} + \alpha_ {n} \mathbf {U} _ {n} ^ {\mathrm{R}} + \beta_ {n} ^ {\mathrm{R}} \mathbf {U} _ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{R}}, \\ \mathbf {H} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {U} _ {n} ^ {\mathrm{L}} = \beta_ {n - 1} \mathbf {U} _ {n - 1} ^ {\mathrm{L}} + \alpha_ {n} \mathbf {U} _ {n} ^ {\mathrm{L}} + \beta_ {n} \mathbf {U} _ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{L}}. \end{array}\tag{9.131}
$$

Apart from initial left and right eigenvectors which must be supplied (and can be taken to be equal, e.g, $U_{i,1}^{L} = U_{i,1}^{R} = 1/\sqrt{N}$ ) the recursions involve only two adjacent $U^{L,R}$ at a time. Rearrangements of Eqs. (9.131) give the residue vectors $\rho_{n}^{L,R}$ and the operational recursion formula,

$$
\begin{array}{r} \rho_ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{R}} = [ \mathbf {H} - \alpha_ {n} ] \mathbf {U} _ {n} ^ {\mathrm{R}} - \beta_ {n - 1} \mathbf {U} _ {n - 1} ^ {\mathrm{R}}, \\ \rho_ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{L}} = [ \mathbf {H} ^ {\mathrm{T}} - \alpha_ {n} ] \mathbf {U} _ {n} ^ {\mathrm{L}} - \beta_ {n - 1} \mathbf {U} _ {n - 1} ^ {\mathrm{L}}, \end{array}\tag{9.132}
$$

from which each successive off-diagonal matrix element $\beta_{n} = T_{n,n + 1} = T_{n + 1,n}$ and vectors $\mathbf{U}_{n + 1}^{\mathrm{L,R}}$ are constructed:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \beta_ {n} = \left([ (\rho_ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{L}}) ^ {\mathrm{T}} \cdot \rho_ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{R}} \right] ^ {1 / 2}, \\ \mathbf {U} _ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{L,R}} = \rho_ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{L,R}} / \beta_ {n}. \end{array}\tag{9.133}
$$

The diagonal matrix elements, $\alpha_{n}=T_{n,n}$ , are obtained from the projection

$$
\alpha_ {n} = \left(\mathbf {U} _ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{L}}\right) ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {H} \mathbf {U} _ {n + 1} ^ {\mathrm{R}}.\tag{9.134}
$$

Note that in principe it is possible that $\left(\mathbf{U}_{n}^{\mathrm{L}}\right)^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{U}_{n}^{\mathrm{R}}=0$ and $U_{n}^{L,R}\neq0$ for a bi-orthogonal vector. However, rounding errors in the computations will always allow a normalization such that $\left(\mathbf{U}_{n}^{\mathrm{L}}\right)^{\mathrm{T}}\mathbf{U}_{n}^{\mathrm{R}}=1.^{13}$

## Answer to Exercise 9.3

Let us carry a similarity transformation of H,

$$
\mathbf {L} = \mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} \mathbf {H A},\tag{9.135}
$$

where

$$
\mathbf {A} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} a & b \\ c & d \end{array} \right)\tag{9.136}
$$

and

$$
\mathbf {A} ^ {- 1} = \frac {1}{\det (A)} \left( \begin{array}{c c} d & - b \\ - c & a \end{array} \right).\tag{9.137}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathbf {L} = \frac {1}{a d - b c} \left( \begin{array}{c c} a d + b c + \mathrm{i} (c d - a b) & 2 b d + \mathrm{i} (d ^ {2} - b ^ {2}) \\ - 2 a c + \mathrm{i} (a ^ {2} - c ^ {2}) & - (a d + b c) + \mathrm{i} (a b - c d) \end{array} \right).\tag{9.138}
$$

Since the matrix is one Jordan block we are left with the following equations:

$$
- 2 a c + \mathrm{i} (a ^ {2} - c ^ {2}) = 0,\tag{9.139}
$$

$$
2 b d + \mathrm{i} (d ^ {2} - b ^ {2}) = a d - b c,\tag{9.140}
$$

$$
a d + b c + \mathrm{i} (c d - a b) = \lambda (a d - b c),\tag{9.141}
$$

$$
- (a d + b c) + \mathrm{i} (a b - c d) = \lambda (a d - b c),\tag{9.142}
$$

where $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue of the matrix. From Eqs.(9.141) and (9.142) it is immediately evident that $\lambda = 0$ , which is indeed the eigenvalue of this matrix. Thus the transformed matrix L is

$$
\mathbf {L} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array} \right)\tag{9.143}
$$

and we have proved here that the matrix H is a Jordan matrix of order 2.

Similarly, one can show that the matrix

$$
\mathbf {L} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \alpha & 0 \\ \gamma & \beta \end{array} \right)\tag{9.144}
$$

can be transformed into a symmetric non-Hermitian matrix, H, by using the transformation matrix

$$
\mathbf {A} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \pm \mathrm{i} a & - a \\ - b & \mp \mathrm{i} b \end{array} \right)\tag{9.145}
$$

and the exceptional point associated with the self-orthogonal eigenvector is obtained when $\alpha = \beta$ .

$$
\text { Answer   to   Exercise   9.4 }
$$

The zero-order eigenvector matrix of the diagonal matrix $H_{0}$ is $\mathbf{C}^{(0)} = \mathbf{I}$ . We set the diagonal elements of $\mathbf{C}^{(n>0)}$ to be equal to zero. That is, $C_{k,k}^{(n)} = \delta_{n,0}$ . As usual in the Rayleigh–Schrödinger perturbation theory, the first-order correction term to the k-th eigenvalue of H is given by

$$
E _ {k} ^ {(1)} = H _ {k, k} ^ {(0)}\tag{9.146}
$$

and the components of the corresponding first-order correction vector to the k-th eigenvector of H are given by

$$
C _ {k, i} ^ {(1)} = \frac {V _ {i , k}}{E _ {k} ^ {(0)} - E _ {i} ^ {(0)}}, \{k, i \} = 1, 2, \dots , N.\tag{9.147}
$$

Let us denote the $(n > 1)$ -order correction terms to the eigenvalues as

$$
E _ {k} ^ {(n + 1)} = \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {N} V _ {k, i} C _ {k, i} ^ {(n)}.\tag{9.148}
$$

We will prove that

$$
C _ {k, i \neq k} ^ {(n)} = \frac {\sum_ {j = 0} ^ {N} (V _ {i , j} - E _ {k} ^ {(1)} \delta_ {i , j}) C _ {k , j} ^ {(n - 1)} - \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {n - 2} E _ {k} ^ {(n - p)} C _ {k , i} ^ {(p)}}{E _ {k} ^ {(0)} - E _ {i} ^ {(0)}},\tag{9.149}
$$

where $\{k, i\} = 1, 2, \ldots, N.$

Proof of Eq. (9.149)

The Rayleigh–Schrödinger perturbation equation is given by

$$
(\mathbf {H} ^ {(0)} - E _ {k} ^ {(0)}) \mathbf {C} _ {k} ^ {(n)} - \sum_ {q = 1} ^ {n} E _ {k} ^ {(q)} \mathbf {C} _ {k} ^ {(n - q)} + \mathbf {V C} _ {k} ^ {(n - 1)} = 0.\tag{9.150}
$$

Let us multiply on the left-hand side of Eq. (9.150) by $[\mathbf{C}_i^{(0)}]^{\mathrm{T}}$ , where $i \neq k$ ,

$$
(E _ {i} ^ {(0)} - E _ {k} ^ {(0)}) C _ {k, i} ^ {(n)} - \sum_ {q = 1} ^ {n} E _ {k} ^ {(q)} C _ {k, i} ^ {(n - q)} + \sum_ {j = 0} ^ {N} C _ {k, j} ^ {(n - 1)} V _ {i, j} = 0.\tag{9.151}
$$

By defining $q = n - p$ , where $p = 1, \ldots, (n - 1)$ , one gets that

$$
\sum_ {q = 1} ^ {n} E _ {k} ^ {(q)} C _ {k, i} ^ {(n - q)} = \sum_ {p = 1} ^ {n - 1} E _ {k} ^ {(n - p)} C _ {k, i} ^ {(p)}.\tag{9.152}
$$

By substituting Eq. (9.152) into Eq. (9.151) one gets Eq. (9.149).

## Answer to Exercise 9.5

The time-dependent Hamiltonian for the interaction of an atom/molecule with an intense linearly polarized laser field and an additional weak field is given within

the dipole approximation by

$$
\hat {H} (\mathbf {r}, t) = \hat {H} _ {\mathrm{system}} (\mathbf {r}) + f (t) \mathbf {e} _ {x} \cdot \mathbf {r} [ \epsilon_ {0} \cos (\omega_ {0} t) + \epsilon_ {1} \cos (\omega_ {1} t) ],\tag{9.153}
$$

where $f(t)$ is the envelope of the laser pulse. The solution of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation (using atomic units where $\hbar = 1$ , e = 1 and $m_{e} = 1$ ),

$$
\hat {H} (\mathbf {r}, t) \psi ((\mathbf {r}, t) = \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t} \psi ((\mathbf {r}, t),\tag{9.154}
$$

can be expressed as a special case of a more general solution:

$$
\psi (\mathbf {r}, t) = \left[ \Psi (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}, t) \right] _ {t ^ {\prime} = t}.\tag{9.155}
$$

$\Psi(\mathbf{r}, t', t)$ is the $(t, t')$ solution for the t-independent Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{r}, t')$ ,

$$
\mathcal {H} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}) = - \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t ^ {\prime}} + \hat {H} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}),\tag{9.156}
$$

and

$$
\Psi (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}, t) = \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \mathcal {H} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}) t} \Psi (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}, t = 0).\tag{9.157}
$$

The use of the $(t, t')$ method enables us to evaluate an analytical expression for the time-evolution operator for the time-dependent Hamiltonian. The reason is clear since $t'$ serves as an additional coordinate. The duration of the two laser pulses is $\tau$ and thus we look for quasi-stationary solutions of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation of the form

$$
\begin{array}{l} \Psi (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}, t) = \exp (- \mathrm{i} E t) \Phi_ {E} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}), \\ \Phi_ {E} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}) = \Phi_ {E} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime} + \tau). \end{array}\tag{9.158}
$$

By substituting Eq. (9.158) into $\hat{H}(t)\Psi(\mathbf{r},t)=\mathrm{i}\partial_{t}\Psi(\mathbf{r},t)$ one gets

$$
\mathcal {H} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}) \Phi_ {E} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}) = E \Phi_ {E} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}),\tag{9.159}
$$

where $\{E+(2\pi/\tau)n\}_{n=\pm1,\pm2,\ldots}$ are also eigenvalues of $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{r},t)$ which are associated with the eigenfunctions $\exp[\mathrm{i}(2\pi/\tau)n]\Phi_{E}(\mathbf{r},t)$ . For this reason we refer to the eigenvalues of the Floquet-type operator $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{r},t)$ as quasi-energies (QE). When r is a contour in the complex coordinate plane (read in Chapter 5 on the complex scaling transformations for which the resonance eigenfunctions are square integrable), the eigenvalues E get complex discrete values. Therefore Eq. (9.159) should be replaced by

$$
\mathcal {H} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime}) \Phi_ {E _ {\alpha}} ^ {\theta} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}) = E _ {\alpha} ^ {\theta} \Phi_ {E _ {\alpha}} ^ {\theta} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}),\tag{9.160}
$$

where $\alpha = 1, 2, \ldots$ and $r_{\theta}$ is one of the contours in the complex coordinate plane described in Chapter 5. The resonance solutions are associated with square integrable eigenfunctions, i.e., $\lim_{r\to\infty}\Phi_{E_{\alpha}}^{\theta}(\mathbf{r},t')=0$ , provided that $\theta$ exceeds a certain value (see Chapter 5), and the corresponding photo-induced resonance eigenvalues,

$$
E _ {\alpha} ^ {\theta} = \mathcal {E} _ {\alpha} - \frac {\mathrm{i}}{2} \Gamma_ {\alpha},\tag{9.161}
$$

are $\theta$ -independent (as long as $\Phi_{E_{\alpha}}^{\theta}$ is square integrable). We can add additional coordinates to the problem by using a similar procedure to that used in the formulation of the $(t, t')$ method. That is,

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {H} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime}, t ^ {\prime \prime}, t ^ {\prime \prime \prime}) = - \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t ^ {\prime}} - \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t ^ {\prime \prime}} - i \partial_ {t ^ {\prime \prime \prime}} + \hat {H} _ {\text {system}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}) \\ \qquad + f (t ^ {\prime \prime \prime}) \mathbf {e} _ {x} \cdot \mathbf {r} _ {\theta} [ \epsilon_ {0} \cos (\omega_ {0} t ^ {\prime}) + \epsilon_ {1} \cos (\omega_ {1} t ^ {\prime \prime}) ]. \end{array}\tag{9.162}
$$

Since the envelope of the laser pulse, $f(t)$ , is a slowly varying function we can apply the adiabatic theorem (read more on it in Chapter 8) where $-i\partial_{t'''}$ is the non-adiabatic coupling potential,

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathcal {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime}, t ^ {\prime \prime}) = - \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t ^ {\prime}} + \hat {H} _ {\mathrm{system}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta})} \\ & {\qquad + f (t ^ {\prime \prime \prime}) \mathbf {e} _ {x} \cdot \mathbf {r} _ {\theta} [ \epsilon_ {0} \cos (\omega_ {0} t ^ {\prime}) + \epsilon_ {1} \cos (\omega_ {1} t ^ {\prime \prime}) ].} \end{array}\tag{9.163}
$$

We will take a laser pulse which supports many optical cycles and thus we can set $f(t^{\prime\prime\prime}) = 1$ , assuming that the envelope of the laser pulse has a trapezoidal shape such that most of the time the laser pulse is at its maximal field amplitude. The adiabatic Floquet-type operator can be further simplified:

$$
\begin{array}{l} \mathcal {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime}, t ^ {\prime \prime}) = - \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t ^ {\prime \prime}} + \mathcal {H} _ {0} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime}) + \epsilon_ {1} \mathcal {H} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime \prime}), \\ \mathcal {H} _ {0} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime}) = - \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t ^ {\prime}} + \hat {H} _ {\text {system}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}) + \epsilon_ {0} \mathbf {e} _ {x} \cdot \mathbf {r} _ {\theta} \cos (\omega_ {0} t ^ {\prime}), \\ \mathcal {H} _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime \prime}) = \mathbf {e} _ {x} \cdot \mathbf {r} _ {\theta} \cos (\omega_ {1} t ^ {\prime \prime}). \end{array}\tag{9.164}
$$

When

$$
\epsilon_ {1} \ll \epsilon_ {0}\tag{9.165}
$$

we can simplify the calculations of the spectrum of $\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{ad}}(\mathbf{r}_{\theta}, t', t'')$ by assuming that the second weak laser couples the two resonance quasi-energy states, $\alpha = 1, 2$ , which are associated with the ground and first excited electronic states of the field-free system (e.g., an atom). These states are solutions of $\mathcal{H}_{0}^{\mathrm{ad}}(\mathbf{r}_{\theta}, t')$ and are given by

$$
\begin{array}{r} \mathcal {H} _ {0} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (\mathbf {r} _ {\theta}, t ^ {\prime}) \Phi_ {\alpha} ^ {\theta} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}) = E _ {\alpha} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} \Phi_ {\alpha} ^ {\theta} (\mathbf {r}, t ^ {\prime}), \\ E _ {\alpha} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} = \mathcal {E} _ {\alpha} - \frac {1}{2} \Gamma_ {\alpha}. \end{array}\tag{9.166}
$$

Using these photo-induced ionizing resonance states as a basis set the $2 \times 2$ Hamiltonian matrix of an atom (or a molecule) which interacts with a combined strong and weak laser fields is given by

$$
\boldsymbol {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (t ^ {\prime \prime}) = \left( \begin{array}{c c} - \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t ^ {\prime \prime}} + E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} \cos (\omega_ {1} t ^ {\prime \prime}) \\ \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} \cos (\omega_ {1} t ^ {\prime \prime}) & - \mathrm{i} \partial_ {t ^ {\prime \prime}} + E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} \end{array} \right),\tag{9.167}
$$

where

$$
d _ {1 2} = \frac {\omega_ {1}}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi / \omega_ {1}} d t ^ {\prime \prime} \left\langle \Phi_ {1} ^ {- \theta_ {1}} \left(t ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \mid \mathbf {r} _ {\theta} \cdot \mathbf {e} _ {x} \mid \Phi_ {2} ^ {\theta_ {2}} \left(t ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \right\rangle_ {\mathbf {r}} = \left\langle \Phi_ {1} ^ {- \theta} (0) \mid \mathbf {r} _ {\theta} \cdot \mathbf {e} _ {x} \mid \Phi_ {2} ^ {\theta} (0) \right\rangle_ {\mathbf {r}}.\tag{9.168}
$$

Since $\boldsymbol{H}^{\mathrm{ad}}(t'') = \mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{ad}}(t'' + 2\pi/\omega_1)$ the eigenfunctions of $\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{ad}}(t'')$ are periodic functions and can be expanded in a Fourier series of $\{\exp(\mathrm{i}\omega_1nt'')\}_{n=0,\pm1,\pm2,\ldots}$ . The Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}^{\mathrm{ad}}(t'')$ is thereby recast as

$$
\boldsymbol {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} \left(t ^ {\prime \prime}\right) = \sum_ {n ^ {\prime}, n} \left| \mathrm{e} ^ {+ \mathrm{i} \omega_ {1} n ^ {\prime} t ^ {\prime \prime}} \right\rangle \left\langle \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \omega_ {1} n ^ {\prime} t ^ {\prime \prime}} \mid \mathcal {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} \left(t ^ {\prime \prime}\right) \mid \mathrm{e} ^ {+ \mathrm{i} \omega_ {1} n t ^ {\prime \prime}} \right\rangle_ {t ^ {\prime \prime}} \left\langle \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \omega_ {1} n t ^ {\prime \prime}} \right|.\tag{9.169}
$$

The Hamiltonian matrix elements are defined accordingly by

$$
\begin{array}{l} [ \boldsymbol {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} ] _ {n ^ {\prime}, n} = \langle \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \omega_ {1} n ^ {\prime} t ^ {\prime \prime}} | \boldsymbol {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (t ^ {\prime \prime}) | \mathrm{e} ^ {+ \mathrm{i} \omega_ {1} n t ^ {\prime \prime}} \rangle_ {t ^ {\prime \prime}} \\ = \frac {\omega_ {1}}{2 \pi} \int_ {0} ^ {2 \pi / \omega_ {1}} \mathrm{d} t ^ {\prime \prime} \mathrm{e} ^ {- \mathrm{i} \omega_ {1} n ^ {\prime} t ^ {\prime \prime}} \boldsymbol {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} (t ^ {\prime \prime}) \mathrm{e} ^ {+ \mathrm{i} \omega_ {1} n t ^ {\prime \prime}} \\ = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \omega_ {1} n + E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} & 0 \\ 0 & \omega_ {1} n + E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} \end{array} \right) \delta_ {n, n ^ {\prime}} + \epsilon_ {1} \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & d _ {1 2} / 2 \\ d _ {1 2} / 2 & 0 \end{array} \right) \delta_ {n, n ^ {\prime} \pm 1}. \end{array}\tag{9.170}
$$

Since the second laser intensity is too weak to support multi-photon processes, we can restrict ourselves to effective one-photon processes where $n'$ , $n = 0$ , $\pm1$ . In such a case, the Hamiltonian matrix is given by

$$
\mathcal {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c c c} E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} + \omega_ {1} & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} + \omega_ {1} & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} - \omega_ {1} & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} - \omega_ {1} \end{array} \right).
$$

When $E_{2}^{ad} - \omega_{1} \simeq E_{1}^{ad}$ and $\epsilon_{1}$ is sufficiently small then it is a good approximation to take into consideration only the coupling between the two almost-degenerate quasi-energy (photo-induced) ionizing resonance states. Under this approximation (which is equivalent to the rotating wave approximation),

$$
\boldsymbol {H} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 \\ \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} - \omega_ {1} \end{array} \right) = E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} \mathbf {I} + \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 \\ \epsilon_ {1} d _ {1 2} / 2 & \Delta E \end{array} \right),\tag{9.171}
$$

where

$$
\Delta E = E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} - \omega_ {1} - E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{ad}} = [ \mathcal {E} _ {2} - \mathcal {E} _ {1} - \omega_ {1} ] - \frac {\mathrm{i}}{2} [ \Gamma_ {2} - \Gamma_ {2} ].\tag{9.172}
$$

This expression is identical to that of

$$
\mathbf {H} = \mathbf {H} _ {0} + \epsilon_ {1} \mathbf {V},
$$

$$
\mathbf {H} _ {0} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \Delta E \end{array} \right),
$$

$$
\mathbf {V} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} 0 & d / 2 \\ d / 2 & 0 \end{array} \right)\tag{9.173}
$$

up to the addition of $E_{1}^{ad}I$ which is equivalent to adding a constant to the eigenvalues. The time-independent Schrödinger equation is

$$
\mathbf {H} \mathbf {C} _ {\pm} = \lambda_ {\pm} \mathbf {C} _ {\pm}.\tag{9.174}
$$

The two eigenvalues of $\mathbf{H}$ are given by

$$
\lambda_ {\pm} = \frac {\Delta E}{2} \pm \frac {1}{2} \sqrt {(\Delta E) ^ {2} + \epsilon_ {1} ^ {2} d ^ {2}}.\tag{9.175}
$$

The two corresponding (c-product) orthogonal vectors are given by

$$
\mathbf {C} _ {\pm} = \mathcal {N} _ {\pm} \binom{1}{[ \epsilon_ {1} d / 2 ] / [ \Delta E - \lambda_ {\pm} ]}.\tag{9.176}
$$

The pre-factors can be taken (with some caution, as will be explained soon) as the normalization factors for which

$$
[ \mathbf {C} _ {\pm} ] ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {C} _ {\pm} = \mathbf {I}\tag{9.177}
$$

and therefore for $\Delta E \neq 0$ and $\epsilon_{1}d \neq 0$ ,

$$
\mathcal {N} _ {\pm} = \sqrt {\frac {1}{1 + \epsilon_ {1} ^ {2} d ^ {2} / (\Delta E - \lambda_ {\pm}) ^ {2}}}.\tag{9.178}
$$

When

$$
\Delta E = \mathrm{i} \epsilon_ {1} d.\tag{9.179}
$$

degenerate eigenvalues are obtained:

$$
\lambda_ {+} = \lambda_ {-} = \frac {\Delta E}{2}.\tag{9.180}
$$

Here we proved that for non-zero off-diagonal matrix element $\epsilon_{1}d$ degenerate eigenvalues can be obtained for a non-Hermitian matrix (note that any matrix can be transformed to be complex and symmetric). It is, however, immediately seen that as the two eigenvalues coalesce also the corresponding eigenvectors coalesce. When we denote the value of $\epsilon_{1}$ for which Eq. (9.179) is satisfied by

$$
\epsilon_ {1} ^ {\mathrm{bp}} = - \mathrm{i} \frac {\Delta E}{d},\tag{9.181}
$$

then Eq. (9.176) is reduced

$$
\mathbf {C} _ {+} = \mathbf {C} _ {-} = \mathcal {N} _ {\pm} \binom{1}{\mathrm{i}}.\tag{9.182}
$$

Using the c-normalization condition for $\epsilon_{1}\neq\epsilon_{1}^{bp}$ as given in Eq. (9.178) one gets that the components of the unit normalized eigenvectors for which $[C_{\pm}]^{T}C_{\pm}=I$ become large and go to $\infty$ as $\epsilon_{1}$ approaches the value of $\epsilon_{1}^{bp}$ .

Only for very special values of the Hamiltonian matrix elements is the branch point, where a single self-orthogonal eigenvector obtained, associated with a real value of $\epsilon_{1}$ ,

$$
\epsilon_ {1} ^ {\mathrm{bp}} = \frac {\operatorname{Re} (\Delta E)}{\operatorname{Im} (d)} = \frac {\operatorname{Im} (\Delta E)}{\operatorname{Re} (d)}.\tag{9.183}
$$

The requirement of a real value for $\epsilon_{1}^{bp}$ results from a physical realization of this case where an atom or a molecule interacts with a combination of strong and weak laser fields. The intensity of the strong laser field $I_{0}$ is much larger than the intensity of the weak almost monochromatic laser field, $[\epsilon_{1}^{bp}]^{2} \ll I_{0}$ with the fundamental frequency $\omega_{bp}$ (using Eq. (9.183)) which is defined by

$$
\hbar \omega_ {\mathrm{bp}} = \mathrm{Re} (E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{QE}} - E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{QE}}) - \mathrm{Im} (E _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{QE}} - E _ {1} ^ {\mathrm{QE}}) \frac {\mathrm{Im} (d)}{\mathrm{Re} (d)},\tag{9.184}
$$

where $E_{1}^{QE}$ and $E_{2}^{QE}$ are the two complex resonance quasi-energy states that are coupled by the weak laser field.

## Answer to Exercise 9.6

(a) Following the explanation in the text, if $\mathbf{c}$ is a defective (self-orthogonal) eigenfunction (eigenvector) of an operator (complex symmetric matrix) $\mathbf{H}$ ,

$$
(\mathbf {H} - E \mathbf {I}) \mathbf {c} = 0,\tag{9.185}
$$

where

$$
\mathbf {c} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \cdot \mathbf {c} = 0,\tag{9.186}
$$

we get for the $2 \times 2$ matrix in Eq. (9.10) that when $\lambda = i$ then $E_{bp} = 0$ and the self-orthogonal vector is

$$
\mathbf {c} = \binom{1}{\mathrm{i}}.\tag{9.187}
$$

Since we have only one eigenvector we can correct the closure relations by adding an additional state d satisfying

$$
(\mathbf {H} - E \mathbf {I}) \mathbf {d} = \mathbf {c},\tag{9.188}
$$

which can be easily solved to yield

$$
\mathbf {d} = \binom{1 / 2}{- \mathrm{i} / 2}.\tag{9.189}
$$

Note that the two non-orthogonal vectors c and d are associated with the same eigenvalue E and satisfy $c^{T} \cdot d = 1$ . It is easy to see that in our case (due to the absence of other orthonormal vectors) we can express the closure relation using these two vectors only and verify that indeed we obtain a unit operator:

$$
\mathbf {I} = \frac {\mathbf {c} \cdot \mathbf {d} ^ {\mathrm{T}} + \mathbf {d} \cdot \mathbf {c} ^ {\mathrm{T}}}{\mathbf {c} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \cdot \mathbf {d}}.\tag{9.190}
$$

(b) Another illustrative example is the $3 \times 3$ matrix which is given in Eq. (9.55) for which

$$
\mathbf {B H B} ^ {- 1} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 6 \end{array} \right),\tag{9.191}
$$

where

$$
\mathbf {B} = \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 0 & - \frac {1}{7} & - 3 \\ \mathrm{i} & - \frac {3 \mathrm{i}}{7} & - \mathrm{i} \\ - 1 & 2 \mathrm{i} & 1 \end{array} \right)\tag{9.192}
$$

The first column, $B_{1}$ , is the self-orthogonal state with eigenvalue of $E_{1}=3\equiv E_{bp}$ . The third column, $B_{3}$ , is the regular state with eigenvalue $E_{3}=6$ . For the second column $B_{2}$ , we find:

$$
\begin{array}{c} (\mathbf {B} _ {2} | \mathbf {B} _ {3}) = \mathbf {B} _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {B} _ {3} = 0, \\ (\mathbf {B} _ {2} | \mathbf {B} _ {1}) = \mathbf {B} _ {2} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {B} _ {1} \neq 0, \\ \mathbf {B} _ {1} = (\mathbf {H} - E _ {1} \mathbf {I}) \mathbf {B} _ {2} \end{array}\tag{9.193}
$$

and one can see that $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are mixed.

For this specific case of Eq. (9.45), $BUB^{T} = I$ , which is satisfied when

$$
\mathbf {U} = \frac {1}{9} \left( \begin{array}{c c c} 8 & - 2 1 & 0 \\ - 2 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{array} \right)  .\tag{9.194}
$$

## Answer to Exercise 9.7

We consider the Hamiltonian

$$
\mathbf {H} = \left( \begin{array}{c c} + 1 & \lambda \\ \lambda & - 1 \end{array} \right)  .\tag{9.195}
$$

Here $\lambda$ is a complex parameter. The eigenvalue problem of H is written as

$$
\mathbf {H} \mathbf {c} _ {\pm} = E _ {\pm} \mathbf {c} _ {\pm}.\tag{9.196}
$$

An explicit calculation gives

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {\pm} = \pm \sqrt {\lambda^ {2} + 1}, \\ \mathbf {c} _ {\pm} = \binom{\frac {\lambda}{E _ {\pm} - 1}}{1}. \end{array}\tag{9.197}
$$

Note that we prefer to keep the eigenvectors un-normalized. The case of $\lambda = i$ corresponds to the branch point, where both the eigenvalues and eigenvectors are degenerate. At the branch point,

$$
\begin{array}{l} E _ {\mathrm{bp}} = 0  , \\ \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} = \binom{- \mathrm{i}}{+ 1}  . \end{array}\tag{9.198}
$$

Moreover, the branch point eigenvector is self-orthogonal, that is, $c_{bp}^{T}c_{bp}=0$ . This explains why we did not implement the usual unit c-normalization.

It is instructive to see how the branch point eigenvector bifurcates into two distinct linearly independent eigenvectors when $\lambda$ is close to i. By expanding the factor $(E_{\pm}-1)^{-1}$ into power series one finds after straightforward manipulations that

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\pm} = \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} \pm \sqrt {\lambda - \mathrm{i}} \binom{1 - \mathrm{i}}{0} + (\lambda - \mathrm{i}) \binom{1}{0} + \mathcal {O} [ (\lambda - \mathrm{i}) ^ {3 / 2} ].\tag{9.199}
$$

Consequently,

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} = \frac {(\mathbf {c} _ {+} + \mathbf {c} _ {-})}{2} + \mathcal {O} [ (\lambda - \mathrm{i}) ].\tag{9.200}
$$

Equation (9.200) shows that the branch point eigenvector can actually be determined quite accurately by combining the two non-degenerate eigenvectors for $\lambda$ close to i. While the difference between $c_{bp}$ and $c_{\pm}$ is of the order $\mathcal{O}[(\lambda - \mathrm{i})^{1/2}]$ , the combination in Eq. (9.200) approximates $c_{bp}$ much better, with an error estimate $\mathcal{O}[(\lambda - \mathrm{i})^{1}]$ . Let us elaborate this point in an alternative way, without directly using the power series expansion of Eq. (9.199). For any $\lambda \neq 0$ we have

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{LC}} = \frac {(\mathbf {c} _ {+} + \mathbf {c} _ {-})}{2} = \binom{\lambda^ {- 1}}{1}.\tag{9.201}
$$

Hence the projection

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{LC}} = 1 - \mathrm{i} \lambda^ {- 1}.\tag{9.202}
$$

On the other hand, the projection

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {\pm} = 1 - \frac {\mathrm{i} \lambda}{E _ {\pm} - 1}.\tag{9.203}
$$

It is convenient to set

$$
\lambda = \mathrm{i} + R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \varphi},\tag{9.204}
$$

where the parameters $R \geq 0$ and $\varphi \in [0, 2\pi]$ characterize the deviation of $\lambda$ from the branch point. Equation (9.202) then boils down to

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{LC}} = \frac {R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \varphi}}{\mathrm{i} + R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \varphi}} = \mathcal {O} (R),\tag{9.205}
$$

whereas the expression in Eq. (9.203) becomes

$$
\mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {\pm} = \mp \sqrt {R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \varphi} (2 \mathrm{i} + R \mathrm{e} ^ {\mathrm{i} \varphi})} + \mathcal {O} (R).\tag{9.206}
$$

This implies that

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial R} \left\{\left| \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{LC}} \right| ^ {2} \right\} _ {R = 0} = 0, \text {but} \frac {\partial}{\partial R} \left\{\left| \mathbf {c} _ {\mathrm{bp}} ^ {\mathrm{T}} \mathbf {c} _ {\pm} \right| ^ {2} \right\} _ {R = 0} = 2 > 0,\tag{9.207}
$$

demonstrating once again that the linear combination $c_{LC}$ is a much better approximation to $c_{bp}$ than $c_{\pm}$ itself.

## Answer to Exercise 9.8

(1) The coalescence of two resonance eigenvalues implies that $E_{\pm}(\epsilon_{0}, \omega_{\mathrm{L}})$ are not analytical functions and thus the Taylor expansions of these functions at the branch point are not applicable. However, the functions $(E_{\pm}(\epsilon_{0}, \omega_{\mathrm{L}}) - E_{\mathrm{bp}})^{2}$ are analytical functions, and when the laser parameters attain values which are sufficiently close to the branch point then the Taylor expansion approach is applicable and the leading term of $(E_{\pm}(\epsilon_{0}, \omega_{\mathrm{L}}) - E_{\mathrm{bp}})^{2}$ is $a(\omega_{\mathrm{L}} - \omega_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{bp}}) +$ $b(\epsilon_{0}-\epsilon_{0}^{\mathrm{bp}})$ . Consequently we can express the two eigenvalues near the branch point by

$$
E _ {\pm} = E _ {\mathrm{bp}} \pm \sqrt {a \Delta \omega + b \Delta \epsilon},\tag{9.208}
$$

where

$$
\begin{array}{l} {\Delta \omega = \omega_ {\mathrm{L}} - \omega_ {\mathrm{L}} ^ {\mathrm{bp}},} \\ {\Delta \epsilon = \epsilon_ {0} - \epsilon_ {0} ^ {\mathrm{bp}}.} \end{array}\tag{9.209}
$$

(2) The condition we wish to fulfill is either

$$
\operatorname{Re} (E _ {+} - E _ {-}) = 0\tag{9.210}
$$

or

$$
\operatorname{Im} (E _ {+} - E _ {-}) = 0.\tag{9.211}
$$

At least one of this conditions must be fulfilled when

$$
\operatorname{Re} \left(E _ {+} - E _ {-}\right) \operatorname{Im} \left(E _ {+} - E _ {-}\right) = 0.\tag{9.212}
$$

On the basis of Eq. (9.208) one gets that this last condition is satisfied to the leading order in expansion whenever

$$
\frac {\Delta \epsilon}{\Delta \omega} = - \frac {a - a ^ {*}}{b - b ^ {*}} = - \frac {\operatorname{Im} (a)}{\operatorname{Im} (b)}.\tag{9.213}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\epsilon_ {0} (\omega) = \epsilon_ {0} ^ {\mathrm{bp}} + \alpha (\omega_ {\mathrm{L}} - \omega_ {\mathrm{L}} ^ {\mathrm{bp}}),\tag{9.214}
$$

where $\alpha = -\frac{\operatorname{Im}(a)}{\operatorname{Im}(b)}$ . Along this line we get that

$$
E _ {+} - E _ {-} = 2 \Delta \omega^ {1 / 2} \left(\frac {\operatorname{Re} (a) \operatorname{Im} (b) - \operatorname{Re} (b) \operatorname{Im} (a)}{\operatorname{Im} (b)}\right) ^ {1 / 2}.\tag{9.215}
$$

(3) Assuming that $[\mathrm{Re}(a)\mathrm{Im}(b)-\mathrm{Re}(b)\mathrm{Im}(a)]/\mathrm{Im}(b)>0$ it is immediately evident from Eq. (9.215) that when $\omega_{L}>\omega_{L}^{bp}$ then $\Delta\omega>0$ and thus $E_{+}-E_{-}$ is real. Thus the only condition which we can satisfy in this case is $\mathrm{Im}(E_{+}-E_{-})=0$ , leading to equal widths for the two resonances. On the other hand, when $\omega_{L}<\omega_{L}^{bp}$ the behavior changes since $E_{+}-E_{-}$ becomes imaginary. In this regime the only condition which can be satisfied is $\mathrm{Re}(E_{+}-E_{-})=0$ and the two resonance have the same energy position. At the branch point both conditions are satisfied and $E_{+}-E_{-}=0$ .

(4) A substitution of Eq. (9.208) into $[\mathrm{Re}(E_{+}-E_{-})]^{2}=[\mathrm{Im}(E_{+}-E_{-})]^{2}$ leads to

$$
\begin{array}{r} \left[ \frac {\sqrt {a \Delta \omega + b \Delta \epsilon} + \sqrt {a ^ {*} \Delta \omega + b ^ {*} \Delta \epsilon}}{2} \right] ^ {2} = \left[ \frac {\sqrt {a \Delta \omega + b \Delta \epsilon} - \sqrt {a ^ {*} \Delta \omega + b ^ {*} \Delta \epsilon}}{2 \mathrm{i}} \right] ^ {2}, \\ a \Delta \omega + b \Delta \epsilon + a ^ {*} \Delta \omega + b ^ {*} \Delta \epsilon = - [ a \Delta \omega + b \Delta \epsilon + a ^ {*} \Delta \omega + b ^ {*} \Delta \epsilon ]. \end{array}
$$

This rearranges to

$$
\Delta \epsilon = - \frac {\operatorname{Re} (a)}{\operatorname{Re} (b)} \Delta \omega .\tag{9.216}
$$

This is just a straight line in the $(\epsilon_{0}, \omega_{\mathrm{L}})$ parameter space given by

$$
\epsilon_ {0} = \epsilon_ {0} ^ {\mathrm{bp}} + \tilde {\alpha} (\omega_ {\mathrm{L}} - \omega_ {\mathrm{L}} ^ {\mathrm{bp}}),\tag{9.217}
$$

where

$$
\tilde {\alpha} = - \frac {\operatorname{Re} (a)}{\operatorname{Re} (b)}.\tag{9.218}
$$
